news.title: The Real Reasons Why Funding For The Democrat Party Is Collapsing
news.text:
Recent polling suggests that expectations of a "blue wave" in Congress for the 2026 mid-terms are crumbling fast, and as we examined recently, the Democrats are facing one of the biggest financial shortfalls in DNC history. The organization has around $16 million of cash on hand for campaign operations after debts are counted. The Republicans have over $129 million cash on hand with zero debt. 

In terms of super-PAC money, the Democrats have $334 million to draw from while Republicans have $1.06 billion.

The funding disparity could not be more obvious, but what is the cause? What happened to the Democrat's massive cash apparatus - the same system that raised over $1 billion for the Kamala Harris campaign in 2024? It's almost as if the money simply disappeared.

Some theories suggest that institutions like USAID were funneling cash into the DNC through various political NGOs and subsidies. There is some validity to these claims.

Groups tied to NGO networks like the former Arabella Advisors (which managed large 501(c) funds handling over a billion dollars for advocacy, ballot measures, and political activity) saw scrutiny and restructuring after Donald Trump took office. These management groups contracted support for Democratic-aligned causes, messaging, voter mobilization, and infrastructure. 

One of the biggest supporters of Arabella Advisors was the Bill Gates Foundation, which cut ties with Arabella last year. Arabella ceased operations in November of 2025 due to investigations into "Dark Money" funding. Interestingly, Democrat coffers have suffered significant declines after Arabella dissolved and rebranded as "Sunflower Services". The organization also had numerous overlapping ties to USAID.

It should also be noted that employee contributions from USAID, the Department of Education and other organizations targeted by DOGE cuts were around 95% Democrat. Huge swaths of the federal bureaucracy have long been run by the far-left. Presidents come and go, but the bureaucracy is forever.

Beyond the dark money angle, much of the DNC's losses can be attributed to their own ideologically unhinged leadership. Kamala Harris, for example, had nearly double the number of billionaire donors and corporate sponsors compared to Donald Trump, yet Trump won the election in a landslide and the Harris camp ended up with $22 million in debt.

Major donors including Bob Kerrigan and Reid Hoffman have pulled back from the DNC after the 2024 disaster, citing lack of faith in leadership and questions over the purpose of the Democratic Party. 

Finally, with the rise of fanatical Democrat Socialist candidates in blue city elections across the US, the Democrat Party is being treated as radioactive. The more the party doubles down on woke, the less people like or trust them (Get Woke, Go Broke). 

It's unclear how well Democrats will perform in the mid-term elections this year given their financial problems, but it is often true that any party that can't get people to vote with their wallets is going to have a hard time getting people to show up at the polls.

news.title: WSJ: Dem Donor Revolt Is Real – and Spectacular
news.text:
Now that the crisis has forced the DNC to postpone payments to vendors, the media has given it more notice. However, the Wall Street Journal took a peek under the hood this weekend and discovered that the fundraising crisis on the Left goes well beyond the DNC. It has become an outright revolt among donors, one that might kneecap the Democrats' midterm hopes:

George Soros and his son Alex donated more than $400,000 to the Democratic National Committee during the 2018 midterms. They gave more than $1 million during the 2022 midterm election cycle, campaign finance records show.This year, they have yet to give the DNC a dollar.The Soroses aren’t alone—other high-profile donors have given little or no money to the Democrats’ central committee this year. Reid Hoffman, the co-founder of LinkedIn, wrote steady checks to the DNC for years but during the midterms has yet to give money.

An underfunded DNC presents a nasty problem for Democrats in the midterms, even if that were the full scope of the problem. The DNC and RNC comprise state committees for each party, which both contribute to and benefit from the organizing power of their national organizations. Candidates for the House and Senate – not to mention in state and local elections – usually lack the organizing and financial resources for get-out-the-vote (GOTV) and other momentum-building activities. The national parties help build those networks so that their candidates can ride on the central structure, using shared resources and streamlining efforts for efficient use of both time and money. The RNC's nine-figure lead in cash on hand puts them well ahead for organization and campaigning, which is why Martin's begging vendors to wait until after the election to get paid for their work now. 

In recent years, however, the national committees have mattered less in these calculations. Thanks to misguided campaign-reform efforts that put arbitrary limits on direct donations to parties and candidates, political power has shifted to PACs and super-PACs instead of the DNC and RNC. The parties' campaign committees probably matter more than their central committees in terms of electoral outcomes, but the PACs and super-PACs may end up mattering more than any of them. The assumption had been that donors had rejected the DNC because of Martin's lack of competence and had just redirected their cash to organizations where Martin's bumbling would have no effect. 

Instead, donors are walking away from the whole structure. The financial boycott has little to do with Martin, as it turns out, and a lot more about being a proxy war between the socialists and the normies:

The DNC isn’t the only problem spot for Democrats—other Democratic committees and super PACs lag behind Republicans across the board. It is common for a party that is out of power in Washington to struggle, but Democrats are increasingly concerned it will hurt their chances of winning this fall as Republicans stack up significantly more money in committees and PACs that can organize door-knocking efforts and air TV ads.Some of the problem is the lingering frustration among major donors over how their money was spent in the 2024 presidential election, when nominee Kamala Harris quickly raised more than $1 billion but still lost after a rushed process to nominate her. Others point to the painful divisions in the Democratic Party’s donor base over the war in Gaza, antisemitism in the U.S. and an insurgent group of Democratic socialists.

The scope of the revolt can be seen in the gaps opening up in these PACs and super-PACs. As the WSJ shows in a graphic on their site, the pro-Trump MAGA Inc super-PAC now has a $400 million war chest, far outstripping official campaign committees from both parties. However, there's no indication that donors are sending money to MAGA Inc as a way to bypass the RNC or Republican Party campaign committees:

National Republican Senatorial Committee has a $56M/$41M edge over the Democratic Senatorial Campaign CommitteeThe GOP's NRCC has $92.7M in the bank, compared to $79M for the DCCCThe main PAC for Senate Republicans has $239 million on hand, almost 2:1 over Dems' $126MThe main PAC for House Republicans has $142M on hand, while Dems' has $90M

Dem donors are not staying entirely on the sidelines, however. Instead, they have directed their funds to specific candidates, with the most stark result in Texas, where James Talarico now has $55 million on hand against Ken Paxton's $4 million. That is a result of a bitter Republican primary and the reluctance of donors to reward Paxton for challenging John Cornyn, which Republicans are trying to resolve before Labor Day. The problem is that Talarico has to spend almost half of that to convince black voters to get over their anger over Talarico's challenge to Jasmine Crockett. A lot of that financial advantage will get spent just to get the party back to the Colin Allred status quo ante, when Allred lost the election by almost ten points to Ted Cruz two years ago. 

Donors are also pouring money into Senate races in Georgia and Ohio, but Democrats are running incumbents in those races, who are facing serious competition in red states too. Donors regularly pour money into these contests, including Texas, so this is not exactly news. In previous cycles, Democrats also had money advantages in the national committees and the PAC/super-PAC front as well. Republicans in these races may benefit from MAGA Inc and the other PACs in play, and they may also get more donors as the primaries end and they can raise general-election funds, which these incumbents have been doing all along. Those wide gaps may not last long, and the PAC support may make them even less relevant.

We have plenty of time between now and November for Democrat donors to change their minds, but for that money to be effective, it needs to arrive before Labor Day. There actually isn't that much time at all for Democrats to resolve their civil war, and there's a good chance that they will burn resources on bad bets in Texas, Michigan, and Wisconsin first.

news.title: From Donald Trump to Abdul El-Sayed: US Arabs centre Palestine in politics  - Jamaica Inquirer – Daily
news.text:
Dearborn, Michigan – Yemeni-American activist Samraa Luqman has no regrets about voting for President Donald Trump in 2024.

While the United States president has been a disappointment to Arab Americans in Michigan with his pro-war and anti-immigration policies, she stressed that it was untenable for the community to vote for Democrats as Israel’s genocide unfolded in Gaza.

“There had to be accountability for the genocide. We’re OK with what we voted for,” Luqman told Al Jazeera.

“I said from the beginning, I’m willing to live through another four years of Trump, that we expected him to be bad on our issues, but it was a pill we were willing to swallow in order to hold the Democratic Party accountable.”

Luqman is not alone.

Despite Trump’s staunchly pro-Israel policies and unpopular war on Iran, many say supporting Democratic nominee Kamala Harris in 2024 was out of the question, and it was the right choice for the community to break with the Democratic Party.

“I could not – with a good heart, good conscience – tell someone to vote for Kamala Harris or Donald Trump”, but the approach of “lesser of two evils” no longer works to sway Arab voters, Hussein Dabajeh, a prominent political strategist in the Detroit area, home to large Arab and Muslim communities, told Al Jazeera.

Democrats’ popularity amongst Arab Americans nosedived in 2024 as President Joe Biden ignored calls to compel a ceasefire in Gaza and continued to provide Israel with weapons and military aid as it killed tens of thousands in Palestine and Lebanon.

Then, Vice President Harris refused even to consider an arms embargo against Israel.

As a result of these policies, many Arab Americans, who had been reliable Democratic voters for years, ditched the party and refused to support Harris in her presidential bid.

Trump swept in, presented himself as a “peace” candidate, and his campaign forged ties with Arab community advocates.

Trump’s policies

At a rally in Michigan ahead of the 2024 vote, Trump brought local Muslim imams to the stage and praised the community.

The Republican leader also visited the predominantly Arab and Muslim Detroit suburb of Dearborn ahead of the election.

Trump ended up winning Michigan as many Arab voters in the Dearborn area refused to back Harris. Some voted for him, while others voted for a third party, left the top of the ticket blank, or skipped the election altogether.

According to an Al Jazeera analysis of election results in heavily Arab precincts in east Dearborn, about 45 percent of the votes went to Trump, 29 percent to Green Party candidate Jill Stein, and 16 percent to Harris.

As president, Trump allowed Israel to continue its attacks on Gaza and Lebanon and launched an unprovoked war against Iran that has sent petrol prices soaring.

He has also intensified the crackdown on Palestinian rights advocacy at home with a campaign to deport noncitizen student activists critical of Israel.

In February, he also terminated immigration protections for Yemeni nationals, sowing fear and uncertainty in a community where many leaders had endorsed him in 2024.

Asked how Arab Americans feel about Trump now, Dabajeh said: “They hate him. There’s no other way of putting it. I don’t think there is a single person I know that voted for Trump from the Arab and Muslim community specifically that looks at what Trump is doing and is happy with what he’s doing, or what he’s done.”

‘The genocide matured us’

Many Arab Americans stress that withholding support for Harris in 2024 was not out of love for Trump.

“No one understands the horrors of Trump’s policy more than us. We were his first victims in 2017,” said Amer Zahr, a comedian and Dearborn Board of Education trustee.

Shortly after starting his first term in 2017, Trump implemented a travel ban on several Muslim-majority countries.

“No one is more aware of the harm that Trump can cause than we are,” Zahr added. “But the genocide matured us in a way that we finally got to the point where we were willing to tell politicians ‘no’.”

As the election season returns to Michigan, Arab Americans once again find themselves at a political crossroads.

The community is rallying behind Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed – who had previously endorsed Harris – but some are keeping their political options open.

Luqman, the Yemeni activist, said she will certainly vote for El-Sayed and Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib – who are outspoken critics of Israel – in the Democratic primary on Tuesday and in the general elections in November.

Luqman said Democratic voters’ support for progressive candidates will help the party regain credibility with Arab voters.

“Those are things that do bring the Democratic Party a little bit of relevance and credibility within our community,” Luqman told Al Jazeera.

“It has kind of brought the community back to centre, whereas they were kind of swinging to the right by a large margin.”

Palestine or bust

While some political commentators have been questioning why US support for Israel has become a decisive issue in US politics, particularly Democratic primaries, the answer in the Arab community is clear.

Advocates say domestic policy takes a backseat when their loved ones are being killed, and their hometowns are being wiped out by their own tax dollars via military aid to Israel.

“Gaza and Palestine and Middle Eastern issues have now become the forefront, the top of everybody’s issues, and it’s become a red line for my community,” Luqman said.

“So if you’re a Republican or Democrat and you hate AIPAC and you value Palestinians’ rights to self-determination, then you’re going to be getting our vote, regardless of what party you’re in,” she said, referencing the powerful American Israel Public Affairs Committee lobby group.

Zahr echoed that message.

“People want us not to be single-issue voters. In other words, they want us to forgo our main issue, get screwed on it, watch our families die because Trump’s bad, and accept all that,” he said.

“Well, we said ‘no’. The blood of the children of Gaza had to mean something.”

Zahr emphasised that Arab Americans are not alone in centring Palestine in their electoral choices, pointing to the defeats that pro-Israel incumbents have suffered across the map in this primary season.

“You’ve gotten to a point where if somebody says, ‘Stop bombing hospitals’, everyone knows you’re talking about Israel. That’s because of Israel. That’s not because of us. That’s because of what Israel did,” he told Al Jazeera.

“And so, people are keying into the truth. And when you learn the truth, something that comes along with that is you learn that you’ve been lied to, and you get angry. A lot of righteous anger is pushing a lot of this.”

Dabajeh, the political strategist, said that while Arab voters care about the economy, affordability and infrastructure – like all Americans – they cannot overlook US policy on Israel.

“Are we supposed to call our family members overseas and be like, ‘Listen, khalto [auntie], this guy over here that’s running for office might kill some of your neighbours, might kill some of your kids, but don’t worry about it, he’s going to take care of the flooding in our homes’?”

“It’s not going to work. We can’t do that.”

Islamophobia and racism

Republicans tried to court Arab and Muslim voters in 2024 and capitalise on the discontent over Gaza policies, but now, many conservatives have returned to demonising the community as an electoral strategy.

Weeks after he was elected, Trump endorsed Randy Fine, a Florida politician with a history of anti-Muslim statements, for Congress. Fine would go on to win and call for the “destruction” of all Muslims.

Meanwhile, Republican governors in Florida and Texas have designated the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) as a “terrorist” group.

In Michigan, Republican Congressman John James, who is running for governor, has also pledged to blacklist the group.

Luqman said James had spoken to community members and promised to engage voters in Dearborn before that announcement.

“There was a really big opportunity for the Republican Party to solidify the swing of the pendulum, if you will, and they lost that option. They really missed that opportunity,” she said.

news.title: Buttigieg Says He's Leaning Toward 2028. Here's What the Numbers Say
news.text: Pete Buttigieg told podcast host Steven Bartlett on The Diary of a CEO that he is "more inclined than not" to run for president again in 2028, a notable shift from the more guarded answers he has given in the past. The former transportation secretary, who finished fifth in the 2020 Democratic primary before Joe Biden secured the nomination, said fatherhood has changed how he weighs the decision. He and his husband, Chasten Buttigieg, adopted twins in 2021. "That's changed all of my equations," Buttigieg said. "It's just something that you really sit with and take seriously, which you should." He stopped short of committing. But six years after his surprise breakout in Iowa, early data suggests Buttigieg would enter a 2028 field as one of its strongest contenders, not a long shot. The Polling Points One Way Buttigieg has topped or placed near the top of nearly every major 2028 Democratic primary survey released this year, though the timing of each poll matters as much as the result. A Manhattan Institute poll taken from July 1 to July 6 found him in third place with 13 percent support, behind former Vice President Kamala Harris at 19 percent and California Governor Gavin Newsom at 15 percent. An Emerson College survey conducted July 19 and 20 put him in first place with 19 percent, ahead of Newsom at 17 percent, along with New York U.S. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Georgia U.S. Senator Jon Ossoff, who garnered 13 percent apiece. Harris trailed at 8 percent. A Public Sentiment Institute survey of Michigan voters, fielded July 25 to July 29, gave Buttigieg 24.2 percent, more than 10 points ahead of Ossoff. Harris drew just 5.1 percent, a steep drop from the 27 percent she held nationally as recently as June and the 33 percent she held in October. A University of New Hampshire Survey Center poll released in February found Buttigieg leading with 20 percent, narrowly ahead of Ocasio-Cortez and Newsom at 15 percent each. Buttigieg also had the highest favorability rating of any potential candidate tested, at 72 percent. Not every poll agrees with the trend line. A UC Berkeley Citrin Center-Politico survey of California voters, fielded February 25 to March 3, had Newsom leading Harris at home, 28 percent to 14 percent, with Buttigieg in fourth at 11 percent, behind Ocasio-Cortez at 12 percent. An earlier Manhattan Institute survey, fielded February 6 to 15, told a similar story nationally: Harris at 23 percent, Newsom at 20 percent and Buttigieg at just 8 percent, before his summer gains. The volatility reflects a field where, in one survey, 16 percent of voters said they remained unsure, and the first primary is still more than 17 months away. Prediction Markets Are Not as Convinced If polling shows Buttigieg surging, prediction markets have been slower to move. As of early August, Polymarket priced Newsom as the favorite for the Democratic nomination at 19 percent, followed by Ocasio-Cortez at 15 percent, Ossoff at 14 percent and Harris at 9 percent. Kalshi's market showed a similar order, with Newsom at 18 percent, Ossoff at 15 percent, Ocasio-Cortez at 14 percent and Harris at 9.5 percent. Buttigieg's own market odds have lagged behind his polling gains, hovering in the mid-single digits for much of the year even as he led individual surveys. Outsider or Establishment? Depends Who's Asking That question sits at the center of Buttigieg's positioning in a primary shaping up around an anti-establishment mood inside the party. Ocasio-Cortez has drawn large crowds touring with Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, an independent, under a "Fighting Oligarchy" banner. Progressive candidate Graham Platner's win over Maine Governor Janet Mills, a Democrat, in a Senate primary and the rise of Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)-aligned candidates in House races have strategists describing the moment as a leftward, anti-incumbent one. Buttigieg has tried to occupy both lanes at once. He praised then-New York City mayoral nominee Zohran Mamdani's "capacity to be a great mayor" and called himself simply a "Buttigieg Democrat" when Fox News pressed him on whether he would disavow DSA positions like abolishing the Senate. At the same time, his 2020 identity as a small-town, Midwestern mayor taking on the Washington field still shapes how some Democratic strategists describe him. "In 2028, the Democratic nominee has to be someone Washington didn't create and can't control," Republican strategist Colin Coley told The Hill, naming Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear as a better fit than establishment-tied figures. Others see Buttigieg differently now. Ettingermentum, a newsletter tracking the invisible primary, dropped him from its top 10 entirely this summer, arguing his "high-effort, low-impact shadow campaign" has struggled against the party's leftward drift. A Manhattan Institute poll found zero percent of Black respondents naming him as their choice, a gap one unnamed Democratic strategist told The Hill he is "clearly trying to fix." The 2020 Precedent Buttigieg’s early strength in 2028 echoes his 2020 rise. He entered that race as a 37-year-old mayor of a city of about 100,000 people, with no statewide or federal office experience and limited national recognition. He went on to win Iowa, narrowly finish second in New Hampshire behind Sanders, and build a national following before Biden’s South Carolina victory reshaped the contest. That history matters in his current standing. New Hampshire Institute of Politics Director Neil Levesque said voters there "focused in on him" once before and appear to be doing so again: "This state was just made for him." The memory of 2020 is part of why Democratic operatives are taking his early numbers seriously, even as prediction markets and other polling point to a crowded and unsettled field. The early data points to Buttigieg as a candidate with clear primary appeal, a significant challenge among Black voters and an unresolved question: whether Democrats in 2028 are looking for an outsider, an insider or someone who can credibly present himself as both. A key part of Buttigieg’s strategy has been frequent appearances on Fox News, where he has debated hosts over U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids, the Iran war and Trump administration policies in a space many Democratic contenders avoid. Strategist Steve Schale said Buttigieg has a rare ability: "He can effectively indict the Trump presidency while still giving Democrats an aspirational vision for the future." Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Edward T. Cummins.

news.title: Peter Buttigieg signals 2028 Democratic presidential bid
news.text:
The race for the White House in 2028 is beginning to take shape, and Pete Buttigieg says he's leaning toward another Democratic presidential campaign.

Appearing on Steven Bartlett's "The Diary of a CEO" podcast on Aug. 3, the former transportation secretary said he is "more inclined than not" to run for president again, though he stressed that many factors could influence his decision.

"I think I'm more inclined than not, but there's so much we don't know," Buttigieg said. "There's so much I don't even know about what's going to happen this year, let alone ... what we need to know later."

Buttigieg also said becoming a parent has changed how he thinks about a potential campaign. He and his husband, Chasten, are raising two adopted children. "That's changed all of my equations," he said. "It's just something that you really sit with and take seriously."

Early 2028 contender

Buttigieg, who finished fifth in the 2020 Democratic primary, remains one of the party's most closely watched potential 2028 candidates.

An Emerson College poll released July 23 showed Buttigieg leading the Democratic field with 19%, narrowly ahead of California Gov. Gavin Newsom at 17%. Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez followed behind.

Other polling has produced different results. A McLaughlin & Associates survey released July 24 found former Vice President Kamala Harris leading the field, with Newsom second. Buttigieg placed fourth at 7%, behind Ocasio-Cortez.

The mixed results underscore how unsettled the Democratic race remains more than two years before the first votes are expected to be cast.

news.title: In Texas, a political group bets $6 million on Latino voters coming back to Democrats
news.text:
A left-leaning group is planning to spend $6 million organizing Latino voters in Texas, a group that has trended away from Democrats but is pivotal to their hopes of picking up seats in Congress.

Somos Votantes has started a $2 million statewide voter education push centered on door-to-door conversations and voter registration. Its affiliated political committee, Somos PAC, is preparing a $4 million advertising campaign focused on three South Texas House districts, where they aim to channel voter angst about the economy into support for Democratic candidates in Republican-leaning districts.

“We’re really hoping that we can reconsolidate support for Democrats by presenting the positive economic vision that Democratic candidates in these House districts have,” said Melissa Morales, the founder of Somos Votantes.

Texas is at the crossroads of the fight for control of the U.S. House in the November midterms, and winning back Hispanics who were drawn to President Donald Trump in 2024 will be key to Democrats’ chances there.

Last fall, Republicans in the Texas Legislature, acting on pressure from Trump, redrew district boundaries in the GOP’s favor, aiming to pick up as many as five Democratic House seats. They made a bet that the decade-long shift of working-class Hispanics toward the GOP was not an aberration, though that’s far from a foregone conclusion.

Somos PAC is targeting three districts where Trump won by double-digit margins in 2024: The 15th District, where Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz is facing Tejano music star Bobby Pulido; the 23rd, which is currently vacant after Republican Rep. Tony Gonzalez resigned after admitting an affair with a staffer who later died by suicide; and the 35th, a largely new district created in the recent redistricting.

Morales said Somos PAC is targeting harder-to-win districts rather than the top-tier battlegrounds getting a flood of national attention. Those districts would make the the difference between Democrats eking out a small majority and running up the score with a 20-seat majority, she said.

“If we’re going to get to that 20, we’re going to have to start investing in some of these more reach districts, and we’re going to have to do it early,” Morales said.

In Texas, that means winning back Latinos.

While Trump gained with Hispanic voters in 2024, opinions of the president have fallen among Hispanics overall since he took office, according to AP-NORC polling. Only 29% of Hispanic adults nationally approved of his performance as president in a June AP-NORC poll, an apparent drop from 41% at the start of his second term.

Latino voters have historically been largely aligned with the Democratic Party but during the 2024 election, they shifted significantly toward Trump. A majority still supported Democrat Kamala Harris for president, but Trump made big gains: 43% of Latino voters nationally voted for him, compared with 35% in the 2020 presidential election, a change attributed in part to their concerns about the economy.

But it’s not enough for former Trump voters to lose faith in the president, Morales said. They need a reason to vote for Democrats, and that’s where the ads come in.

“We risk people staying home because they’re disillusioned about everything,” she said.

news.title: Ousted ‘60 Minutes’ stars Scott Pelley and Sharyn Alfonsi reveal their next gigs
news.text:
Those who can’t do, teach.

Axed “60 Minutes” correspondents Scott Pelley and Sharyn Alfonsi will serve as “journalists in residence” at Columbia University.

The Ivy League uni said Monday that the duo — who got the boot from the prestigious show amid a sweeping shake-up under CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss — will work with students via lectures, workshops and special events.

They will each contribute a piece to the high-minded Columbia Journalism Review, too.

The move comes just two months after Pelley’s highly-publicized firing and after Alfonsi’s contract expired following her own public scrap with Weiss.

“We’re both excited and honored to welcome two journalists of this caliber to our Journalist in Residence Program,” Columbia’s J-School Dean Jelani Cobb said in a statement. 

“Their distinguished track records in investigative reporting highlight the amazing opportunity our students will have to learn from them, and we look forward to having Sharyn and Scott with us this year.”

Pelley was fired for cause from CBS in early June, after he tore into “60 Minutes'” new executive producer Nick Bilton over his lack of experience during a staff meet-and-greet.

Pelley also accused Weiss — who was not present at the pow-wow — of “murdering ’60 Minutes.'”

In a memo announcing Pelley’s exit, Bilton said the journalist “hijacked” his first meeting with staffers and showed a total unwillingness to collaborate moving forward.

Pelley’s anger was sparked by upheaval days earlier, when correspondents Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega, executive producer Tanya Simon and senior producers Draggan Mihailovich, Guy Campanile and Matthew Polevoy, headed for the exit.

CBS News let Alfonsi’s contract expire in late May amid complaints from the reporter of “corporate meddling” in her work.

Alfonsi spoke out against Weiss’ last-minute decision to hold one of her pieces on El Salvador’s notorious CECOT prison, and Vega has since griped that management attempted to insert “political bias” into her stories.

CBS News has denied Vega’s claim, and Alfonsi’s story eventually did air in January, with few changes apart from a new introduction and postscript from the correspondent.

After his defenstration, Pelley told “The New York Times” that the network’s management “instructed me to inject falsehoods and bias into a politically sensitive story.”

At the time, a CBS News rep said that what occurred was the normal back-and-forth of the editing process.

As previously reported by The Post, Pelley, Alfonsi and other fired staffers are mulling launching their own version of “60 Minutes” with longtime former executive producer Bill Owens. 

They are looking to raise $50 million to fund two years’ worth of in-depth and investigative news segments, sources with knowledge of the matter said.

Owens – who resigned last year as “60 Minutes’” executive producer amid a dustup between CBS and President Trump over how a Kamala Harris interview was edited – is reportedly penning a scorched-earth memoir about the network.
news.summary: Pelley and Alfonsi -- who both exited the prestigious newsmagazine show amid a sweeping shake up under CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss -- are donning prof gowns.

news.title: New California law will change the internet forever as ‘digital fingerprints’ added
news.text:
California is putting a digital leash on AI fakes.

A landmark new state law taking effect this week will require artificial intelligence companies to add invisible “digital fingerprints” to AI-generated images, videos and audio, giving users a way to determine whether the content they’re seeing was made by a human — or a machine.

Written by Bay Area lawmakers, it will require AI companies to embed difficult-to-remove data known as “provenance” into their creations, allowing people to check a file’s origins through content verification tools.

The goal is to make the internet a little less of a Wild West.

“While AI has some benefits, we’ve seen AI content used for election misinformation for scams and abusive deepfakes,” state Sen. Josh Becker, D-Menlo Park, recently told KQED.

The concern comes as AI-generated political content has already begun making waves in The Golden State.

As previously reported by The Post, two California Democrats recently urged Congress to crack down on AI-generated campaign ads that could impersonate candidates or political organizations as the technology becomes increasingly sophisticated.

US Sen. Adam Schiff and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Fremont) are pushing a new crackdown that would stop fake candidate impersonations from hijacking federal campaigns.

The push came after California political campaigns embraced AI-generated ads.

This included Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton’s videos attacking Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Democratic nominee Xavier Becerra — as well as former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt’s viral “Pratt Man” campaign video, which racked up millions of views with a Hollywood-style AI parody.

Schiff warned that AI-fueled political deception crosses party lines.

“AI-generated fraudulent advertising which uses the likeness or voices of candidates to misrepresent their positions, campaigns, or causes, or otherwise misrepresents a candidate’s point of view is not only wrong — it poses a serious threat to our democracy that should concern all Americans regardless of their party,” Schiff said.

While some fakes aim to fool the public, these West Coast campaign clips wore their digital DNA on their sleeves, utilizing Tinseltown-style animation and satire.

Still, as machine-made political content floods the internet, the line between fact and fiction is getting harder for voters to see.

Becker teamed up with Assemblymember Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, and Rick Chavez Zbur, D-Los Angeles, on the law, aiming to give everyday internet users a fighting chance in a world where AI fakes can look eerily real.

Starting this Sunday, Aug. 9, users will be able to upload an image, video or audio file into a content verifier — such as one created by the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity — to check whether it was created by AI.

The law’s rollout won’t stop there. Come Jan. 1, 2027, Big Tech will have to give users a way to unmask AI-made content hiding in plain sight.

By 2028, phones and cameras manufactured in California will also be required to store provenance information at the moment an image is captured, essentially giving every photo its own digital birth certificate.

The law may have passed in 2024, but getting it off the runway took nearly three years as lawmakers tried to catch up with AI’s breakneck evolution.

California lawmakers also worked closely with officials in the European Union while developing the rules, with the law taking effect the same day as the EU’s new AI Act.

While the first phase of the law primarily targets AI companies, experts say the biggest impact could come when the rules reach social media platforms.

Stephen Sharp Queener, an academic researcher with Starling Lab, warned that the platform requirements could reshape how people consume information online.

If enforced, the rules “will no doubt have a larger effect on our information economy,” Queener wrote in a recent Substack post.

As AI-generated content floods the internet, California is betting that the best defense against digital deception is transparency — putting a tiny digital trail behind every synthetic creation.

Because in the age of AI, seeing isn’t always believing.

news.summary: The goal is to make the internet a little less of a Wild West.

news.title: Democrat Jake Johnson, a teacher, tries to solve the difficult math in a red district
news.text:
NEW ULM, Minn. – Years ago, a teacher who had never run for political office tried to unseat a Republican who seemingly had a lock on Minnesota’s 1st Congressional District.

The Democrat, who is now Gov. Tim Walz, succeeded in 2006 in unseating the Republican, former Rep. Gil Gutknecht, in that largely rural southern district that leans strongly towards the GOP.

Now, like Walz did 20 years ago, another teacher new to politics is running as a Democrat to try to unseat another Republican incumbent.

He’s Jake Johnson, whose campaigning prowess and ability to raise campaign cash has caught the attention of the national Democratic Party. Johnson, 42, hopes to unseat Rep. Brad Finstad, the Republican who now holds the 1st District seat. 

Related: In a tough election year for House Republicans, Brad Finstad faces a serious challenge from Jake Johnson

But unlike the last time a Democrat unseated a Republican in the district, it has changed and so has American politics.

And while Walz and Johnson share similarities, each man is different. 

Both leveraged their years as longtime teachers in the district to broaden their support, among former students and the politically powerful teachers’ unions.

Walz, a history teacher and football coach in Mankato, ran as a moderate Democrat, even as some 1st District voters complain that he became more liberal after winning the governor’s office. Johnson is also running in the district as a centrist.

He is trying to position himself as a fiscal conservative, promising to vote against any legislation that would allow the federal government to borrow more money until Congress balances its budget.

“Members of both parties are not taking this seriously,” he said of the nearly $40 trillion national debt.

But, like most mainstream Democrats, Johnson has also promised to shore up the federal social safety net.

As governor, Walz also focused on expanding social welfare programs, spending his political capital on providing universal school breakfasts and lunches and a generous paid family leave program.

Both men were raised in families that needed the help of social welfare programs.

Johnson, a high school math teacher, grew up in Stewartville with 10 siblings. He says his father collected garbage and his mom went door-to-door reading meters.

The family often needed the help of their church and neighbors and the support of government programs. “I was a SNAP (food stamp) kid,” he said. “We were a Medicaid family.”

Walz also experienced hardship as a youth. After his father died, his mother and younger brother depended on Social Security survivor benefits for support.

‘Red to Blue’ 

Pat Booker, a voter in the district, watched Walz’s rise and is closely following Johnson’s. She said each of them brought skills from their classrooms to the campaign trail.

“(Johnson) doesn’t hesitate to answer questions and doesn’t hesitate to meet with constituents, and that was the same way with Tim,” she said. “That’s something that Brad absolutely refuses to do.”

She would know, having tried and failed to get facetime with Finstad over the course of eight months. Concerned about SNAP and Medicaid cuts, the New Ulm resident went to Finstad’s local congressional office multiple times per week seeking answers.

“I got one pat letter saying thank you for your concerns,” said Booker, a military veteran and retired probation officer. 

There may be a reason Finstad is confident in winning reelection, besides the clear advantages of the makeup of his district and incumbency, which includes heightened name recognition and, usually, greater ability over a challenger to fundraise.

“He’s certainly acting like internal (campaign) polls are telling him he has a wide lead,” said Kevin Parsneau, a political science professor at Minnesota State University in Mankato.

Finstad, 50, lives in New Ulm, a city that holds tight to its German heritage. A statue of the ancient Germanic hero Hermann towers over the city, a glockenspiel chimes every day downtown and August Schell’s brewery holds popular Oktoberfest and Bock Fest events. The German language is conspicuous, adding flavor to the names of bakeries, restaurants and other businesses.

Some locals still trace their lineage to the city’s founding in 1854. There’s even a group known as the Junior Pioneers of New Ulm and Vicinity that celebrates the direct descendants of pioneers who settled in the area by 1870. 

In a city steeped so much in history and heritage, though, locals say newcomers can find it hard to shed an “auslander” label, the German word for “outsider.” Booker, who has lived in New Ulm for decades, said the community has become more open minded and welcoming over time. 

Yet New Ulm definitely remains a conservative, Republican-majority city. It is the county seat of Brown County, which President Donald Trump handily won over former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024.

Even so, Johnson has been taking the race to Finstad’s home turf. He walked in New Ulm’s Bavarian Blast festival parade in July and will hold a town hall in the city in August.

An underdog in Trump territory 

There’s no doubt Johnson is the underdog in the race.

The district gave Trump 55% of the vote in 2024 and GOP incumbent Finstad has deftly defeated his Democratic challengers since he won a special election for the 1st District seat in 2022.

But Johnson has recently received some vital help from the national Democratic Party. 

Mindful of his campaigning skills — which include holding town halls in each of the district’s 21 counties — and especially of his fundraising skills, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) has recently placed Johnson on its “Red to Blue” list.

Those on the list are the Democratic candidates who are trying to flip a Republican-held seat and are considered worthy enough of the national Democratic Party’s help.

The “Red to Blue” designation gives candidates access to fundraising support, strategic guidance and training.

Johnson has already proven himself a strong fundraiser, having amassed nearly $1.9 million in campaign funds as of June 30, the latest reports filed with the Federal Election Commission show.

Finstad, meanwhile, has raised nearly $2 million.

Democrats hope Trump’s low approval ratings, an energized Democratic base and the historic advantage the party out of power in the White House holds in midterm elections will allow them to wrest control of the U.S. House from the GOP.

To do that, Democrats need to win in swing districts. They also hope to increase their numbers in the U.S. House by toppling Republican incumbents in places like the 1st District, which the Cook Political Report rates as “likely Republican.” 

When Walz flipped the seat, it had been held by Gutknecht, a moderate Republican. Finstad, meanwhile, has closely aligned himself with Trump. 

And redistricting, the GOP’s sharp turn to the right and the influence Trump has on local elections has made the 1st District much more difficult territory for Democrats since Walz ran to represent it.

“It’s gotten a lot more conservative,” said Kate Knutson, a political science professor at Gustavus Adolphus College.

Redistricting has a little to do with that. After Census-mandated changes, the district grew even more rural when it picked up new territory in the south of the state along the Mississippi River.

The area has also been impacted by a national trend: rural areas of the United States becoming more Republican as their residents grow concerned that their cultural values – church, family and freedom from government interference – are threatened by a rapidly changing nation. 

Social scientists also say that many rural residents also believe that the Democratic Party is composed of urban elites who look down on rural lifestyles and prioritize city or immigrant populations over rural working-class struggles. 

Knudson said the “farmer” part of the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party has “peeled off.”

But she said Johnson might succeed in depressing – at least a little bit – the enthusiasm among farmers for the GOP by continuing to hammer Finstad for embracing Trump policies that have hurt farmers.

“Farmers are frustrated by tariff and immigration sweeps that are hurting the meat packing industry in southern Minnesota,” Knutson said.

Iran’s shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz, which has stalled significant deliveries of oil and fertilizer, raising the cost of farm inputs, has also taken a toll in farm country.

Related: Minnesota progressives campaign on ‘Medicare for All’ as ranks of uninsured grow. Moderates – including Jake Johnson – embrace less ambitious reforms.

Finstad has brushed off criticisms of Trump’s policies on agriculture and has blamed former President Biden for the distress.

“We’re heading in the right direction,” he told MinnPost after a roundtable on veterans’ issues in Mankato in July. “We have come out of some tough times where the inputs have been really crippling for the last six years, and then on top of that we’ve had that stale market because of that lack of trade.”

Speaking to his base 

Although Johnson is proving to be a growing threat, Finstad avoids acknowledging his challenger, preferring instead to hold events in the district that can be classified as official business, including meeting with police officers, farm groups and local companies.

“He’s speaking to his base,” Parsneau said. “He does not want to be in an unscripted situation.”

Yet Finstad told MinnPost that “he travels all over southern Minnesota.”

“I’m always listening and communicating with constituents who agree and don’t agree with me,” Finstad said. “I’m having those conversations and I would say reach out to me, reach out to our office. I’m more than willing to have a conversation and answer questions.”

Finstad also said it is “an honor of a lifetime” to serve the 1st District’s 750,000 residents, “but my goal is heaven, not Congress.”

“When November comes, the voters of southern Minnesota will decide, but no one is going to outwork me,” Finstad said.
news.summary:
Another teacher, Tim Walz, was the last Democrat to flip the rural southern Minnesota district that’s now held by Republican Brad Finstad.

news.title: What's on voters' minds as hard-fought Democratic US Senate primary approaches
news.text:
The race for the Democratic nomination for Michigan's open U.S. Senate seat between former health director Abdul El-Sayed of Ann Arbor and U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens of Birmingham has been hard-fought, caustic and expensive, drawing national attention and swamping Michigan airwaves with campaign attacks and advertisements.

And it's about to conclude after polls close at 8 p.m. Tuesday, Aug. 4 and the counting gets underway to determine whether El-Sayed, a progressive firebrand, or Stevens, the experienced centrist, takes on Republican former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers of White Lake (who was unopposed in his primary) in a November general election that could help decide which party controls the chamber.

Voting in Michigan, by absentee ballot and by early in-person voting, has been underway for some weeks, and we went out to talk to Democratic primary voters to hear who they were supporting in this vitriolic race and why:

'About the policies he wants to implement'

Jay Joseph, 22, of East Lansing, who is studying medical billing and coding at Lansing Community College, voted by absentee ballot for El-Sayed, saying, "People have been wanting some more progressive politics from the Democrats for a long time, so I’m really proud to vote progressively this time around. I hope everybody else does.”

Joseph also said that she's more impressed with El-Sayed's campaign ads, saying they seem more "about the policies he wants to implement. " Stevens' ads, Joseph said, "are just attacks on someone else, and I haven’t heard much about her own policies.”

— Paul Egan

'Obama backed her up'

Esther Doyle, 63, of Detroit, said a few days before the election she had voted for Stevens. “She's been around awhile, and (former President Barack) Obama backed her up,” she said. When a Free Press reporter noted that, despite Stevens' working as a member of his auto rescue team in 2009-10 (and TV ads which may suggest otherwise), Obama hasn't endorsed anyone in this race, Doyle said, “Not yet."

Doyle contrasted Stevens’ experience with El-Sayed’s emergence on the political scene. “Just out the blue. I never heard of him ever before,” she said. “I never knew anything about him period until he just showed up on my TV."

— Clara Hendrickson

'He doesn't take AIPAC money'

Marianne Krist, 65 of Detroit, said she voted for El-Sayed. “He doesn’t take AIPAC money," she said, referring to the American-Israel Public Affairs Committee, a pro-Israeli lobbying group that has, through another organization, spent tens of millions supporting Stevens and attacking El-Sayed. "He’s progressive and that’s about it,” she said.

"Nothing against her but it’s time for progressive changes, you know?" Krist said. She said she would back Stevens if she wins the nomination but she's not swayed by Stevens' argument she may be more electable than El-Sayed in the November general election. “That’s not enough reason for me to vote for her, and honestly I think the momentum is on El-Sayed’s side at this point."

— Clara Hendrickson

'I'm with Haley'

Josephine Purnell-Parker, 56, of Sterling Heights, is a centrist Democrat who opposes government-run healthcare (which El-Sayed supports). She also said El-Sayed and others who supported the Uncommitted movement to send a signal to then-President Biden's administration about their opposition to U.S. aid to Israel helped elect Republicans to Congress and the White House in 2024. (El-Sayed, while supporting the Uncommitted movement in the primary season, fully supported Vice President Kamala Harris when Biden stepped down and she became the Democratic nominee.)

"I'm with Haley," she said. "But if El-Sayed wins, I’m not going to vote uncommitted because that’s hurting myself. They need to think about that. When you try to divide us, you’re hurting all of us. We need to be united.”

— Tristan McFolley

'They got money to throw away on a stupid war'

Sean Morris, 63 of Sterling Heights, said he voted for El-Sayed because of the candidate's support for a government-run healthcare plan that would cover all Americans, also known as Medicare for All. “We need healthcare for one thing,” Morris said. “My insurance got yanked, and from what I keep hearing from my relatives, it’s going to be a mountain of paperwork just to move to Canada.”

Morris believes El-Sayed's platform is a marked change from the status quo. “They got money to throw away on a stupid war (referring to the Trump administration's war with Iran) and yet they can’t afford to feed people or afford healthcare (for everyone).”

— Tristan McFolley

'Well, I don't know him'

Myra Jefferson-King, 73 of Detroit, said she voted for Stevens in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate. She traced her reasoning for supporting Stevens to the fact that Jefferson-King had campaigned for Gov. Gretchen Whitmer in the past and Whitmer endorsed Stevens in the Senate race.

But she didn’t describe her vote as an anti-El-Sayed vote. “Well, I don’t know him,” she said.

— Clara Hendrickson

'This has been a super nasty race'

Jason Wade, 52, of Bloomfield Township, cast his vote early for El-Sayed. “The economy isn’t working for working people and he has a vision for that,” said Wade, who works for the United Auto Workers (which has endorsed El-Sayed).

Wade is confident El-Sayed will win both the primary and general elections but has concerns about the lingering effects of an acrimonious primary season for Democrats. “I think this has been a super nasty race," he said. "I think it’s off-putting to most Michiganders how much money has come in from out of state, and hopefully this is seen as a warning for November and (the presidential election in ) ’28. We can make our own decisions."

— Emily Lawler

Contact Todd Spangler: tspangler@freepress.com. Follow him on X @tsspangler. Staff writers Paul Egan, Clara Hendrickson, Emily Lawler and Tristan McFolley compiled the interviews for this story.

news.title: Kamala Harris leaves Biden off list of top three 'most effective' presidents
news.text: Former Vice President Kamala Harris left former President Joe Biden off a list of her top three most effective U.S. presidents in an interview on Friday. "In your view, rank the top three most effective presidents in American history," Marc Morial, the president of the National Urban League, asked Harris at the National Urban League conference on Friday. She joked, "Marc, don't make me do that." Harris then went on to name Franklin Delano Roosevelt (FDR) as her first pick and said she watched an NPR special about him recently. KAMALA HARRIS IS THE 'FAIRLY OBVIOUS' 2028 PRESIDENTIAL FRONTRUNNER, DEMOCRATIC INSIDERS SAY "It was he who talked about the expansion of the Supreme Court, and then he got ferocious back — kind of blowback for that. But he did good. It was Social Security. It was, you know, when I think about what he did in terms of investing in the people in during dire times and talking about the role and responsibility of government, that it should not just be about the benevolence of community organizations or just interpersonal relationships, that the government has a role. I think that he was a very important president," she said. She went on to name John F. Kennedy — also noting Lyndon B. Johnson, Kennedy's vice president, who took over the presidency after he was assassinated. "I credit, you know, Kennedy, of course, in terms of what he laid the groundwork for and then Johnson followed up on," she said. "Around having the ability, but that was again an example of the inside outside game. Because the reason that happened is because the pressure was on from the outside to appeal to the conscience of the people on the inside." HILLARY CLINTON STILL FUMING OVER ELECTORAL COLLEGE, CALLS IT AN 'ABOMINATION' IN NEW NETFLIX SERIES Harris listed Barack Obama as her third choice, which the audience applauded. "What he did with the Affordable Care Act among many things, but in particular, if we had one issue that has been ailing America for generations, which is a healthcare system that has failed anyone other than the rich and addressing that the way that he did and took a lot of heat for it. I think it's one of the greatest presidents," Harris said. The list notably left off Biden, under whom she served as vice president. Neither Harris' office nor Biden's office immediately returned Fox News Digital's requests for comment. Harris took Biden's spot at the top of the Democratic presidential ticket in 2024 after the former president decided to exit the race following a rough debate performance against now-President Donald Trump. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Harris had a little over 100 days to mount a presidential campaign, and wrote in her book after the election that his decision to run for a second term was reckless. "'It’s Joe and Jill’s decision.' We all said that, like a mantra, as if we’d all been hypnotized. Was it grace, or was it recklessness?" Harris wrote. "In retrospect, I think it was recklessness. The stakes were simply too high. This wasn’t a choice that should have been left to an individual’s ego, an individual’s ambition. It should have been more than a personal decision." Harris took a series of left-wing policy positions during the conversation, and said she had not made a decision about 2028 yet. "We must allow for a real conversation about revisiting certain things," Harris said. "I know this is gonna be controversial coming from me, in particular. We need to revisit the Electoral College." Harris lost both the Electoral College and the popular vote to President Donald Trump in the 2024 election. She also voiced support for expanding the Supreme Court. "We need to revisit the point of expanding the court to 13 justices, like we have 13 district courts," Harris said. She also suggested the U.S. should revisit statehood for Puerto Rico, expanding beyond her previous support for statehood for Washington, D.C. Zeteo founder and far-left commentator Mehdi Hasan reacted to a clip posted of Harris with a Biden animation where he appeared surprised. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Independent's Eric Michael Garcia also reacted with a gif of the former president.
news.summary: Harris praised FDR's, JFK's and Barack Obama's legacy in her list of the most effective presidents, but notably left out the president she served under as vice president.

news.title: Kamala Harris Introduces 'Controversial' Plan For Democrats To Beat 'Cheating' Republicans
news.text:
Kamala Harris knows that Democrats have to do more to win big elections. 

During a fireside chat at the National Urban League’s annual conference in Nashville last week, the former vice president discussed the party’s strategy for the upcoming midterm and presidential elections ― and the high stakes that Democrats are facing. 

“Registering folks to vote and having an agenda that is about turning out the vote in the greatest numbers we have ever seen so that in this environment where they are cheating, we will be too big to rig,” Harris said to applause from the crowd when asked about how Democrats can respond.

“It means being ruthless. They are ruthless,” she said of Republicans. “We need to be ruthless, too. And by that, I do not mean cruel. That is not our nature. By that, I do not mean breaking the law. That is not what we do. But I do mean we must be uncompromising.” 

Harris then postured that the party “must allow for a real conversation about revisiting certain things” before offering up her ideas. 

“I know this is going to be controversial coming from me in particular. We need to revisit the Electoral College,” she said to more applause. “We need to revisit the point of expanding the court to 13 justices, like we have 13 district courts. We need to revisit, if they so want, statehood for Puerto Rico and D.C.” 

Harris hasn’t ruled out a future run for the 2028 presidential election.

“I am not done,” Harris told the BBC last year. “I have lived my entire career as a life of service, and it’s in my bones.”

news.title: Ex-60 Minutes boss wants to create rival broadcast with fired staffers: report
news.text:
A former producer of CBS News’s 60 Minutes is interested in launching a rival current affairs show featuring journalists and production crew members who left the network now spearheaded by Bari Weiss, according to a report.

The long-running investigative news show has been in turmoil ever since Weiss was appointed editor-in-chief of CBS’s news division last year, suffering internal tensions, sliding ratings and a series of departures – notably losing anchor Scott Pelley – as the new boss tried to address its alleged liberal bias.

Producer Bill Owens left 60 Minutes last April, prior to Weiss’s arrival, amid an earlier dispute with President Donald Trump about the editing of an interview with his 2024 presidential rival Kamala Harris that aired in the run-up to Election Day.

He is now looking to pick up the pieces, according to The New York Post, and is seeking $50 million in funding to launch a new hour-long news program manned by some of the staff Weiss allegedly alienated and jettisoned, including Pelley, which he is said to have been shopping around to the major streaming platforms.

Ex-correspondents Sharyn Alfonsi and Cecilia Vega, former executive producer Tanya Simon and senior producers Guy Campanile, Draggan Mihailovich and Matthew Polevoy are also tipped to be part of the project.

A source close to Owens denied the plans and the producer himself declined to comment, the Post noted, but it cites other sources that say fired 60 Minutes staffers have put together a business plan and pitch deck for consideration by Netflix, Apple TV and YouTube.

Securing the funding and finding the right platform would be crucial to any such venture’s success, with the likes Pelley likely to have to take a significant pay cut in order to take part.

“I think they’re asking for too much money,” an insider said to be familiar with the project told the newspaper. “They’re looking at the old 60 Minutes model and they’re all used to mega salaries.”

Without the backing of a top streamer such as Netflix, a proposed show would have to operate on a shoestring budget and build a new subscriber base from scratch, a notoriously tricky proposition.

Weiss arrived at CBS in October when Paramount Skydance acquired her media company, The Free Press, for a reported $150 million – but her tenure quickly became defined by controversy and upheaval.

The discontent engulfed 60 Minutes in December when she delayed the airing of a segment alleging that “brutal and torturous conditions” prevailed at CECOT, the El Salvador mega-prison where the Trump administration has deported migrants.

The official verdict was that the piece “needed additional reporting” but the journalist involved, Alfonsi, insisted that best practice had been followed throughout. The report eventually aired with only minor changes on January 18.

Alfonsi was fired in May alongside Vega and Simon, leading Pelley to explode at the latter’s successor, Nick Bilton, during an editorial meeting, accusing Weiss of “murdering” the show. He was quickly shown the door after the blow-up.

Weiss has also been blamed for sidelining veteran anchor Lesley Stahl and giving more airtime to hand-picked Tony Dokoupil.

Bilton is said to have been upset at being rebuked by Pelley, who reportedly belittled his “slender qualifications,” and to have struggled to hire replacements for the talent lost.

However, he announced last week that New York Times columnist Ross Douthat, author Sebastian Junger, Vice News veteran Gianna Toboni and British commentator Trevor Phillips would all be joining its presenting roster, along with network veteran Norah O’Donnell.

Pelley and Alfonsi have meanwhile just been announced as Columbia University’s journalists-in-residence, describing their appointments as an “extraordinary privilege.”
news.summary: A new current affairs program is reportedly being pitched to streaming giants and could involve talent frozen out or dismissed by controversial CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss

news.title: DNC Autopsy Author Says Party Omitted Key Section From Public Draft: NYT
news.text:
Paul Rivera, the author of the Democratic National Committee’s autopsy on why the party lost the 2024 presidential election, said the lengthy draft the DNC made public in May left out an important section, The New York Times reported on Monday, as the party continues to grapple with internal tensions ahead of the crucial midterm elections.

Rivera told The Times he hand-delivered the chapter to embattled DNC chairman Ken Martin in January, but Martin denies that ever happened.

“This alleged report section was not in any binder I reviewed,” Martin told the outlet. 

“If we had this in May, we would have released it with the rest of the report,” he added.

The chapter, titled “What Happened In 2024,” which was published in full by the Times, pointed to former President Joe Biden’s decision to pursue reelection as well as the financial situation of Democratic campaign operatives as some of the contributing factors to the party’s failure to win.

Rivera writes that Democrats’ better-than-expected performance in the 2022 midterms led them “to believe they were stronger than they actually were” and also prompted Biden to make the “consequential” call to run for a second term.

“Is there a single point of failure for 2024?” Rivera asked. “Perhaps it is a decision of the President to seek re-election instead of passing the torch, but Democrats do not have a time machine to go back and change his decision, and the particular circumstances of the 2023-2024 political landscape will likely never happen again.”

The passage released by The Times also says that many of the people who worked at the highest levels of the party and the presidential campaign itself were either too wealthy or privileged to grasp the struggles of everyday Americans.

“They missed important signals about why people were frustrated with Democrats, who seemed not to appreciate or understand their situation,” the chapter reads.

This latest dispute, revealed by The Times, comes as Martin is under growing pressure to step down over the party’s dire financial situation, among other issues, with the key November midterm elections looming.

Martin has also faced sharp criticism over the handling and the quality of the report Rivera authored. While Martin originally pledged to publish the autopsy, he backtracked before eventually releasing it to CNN, acknowledging it was deeply flawed.

The autopsy included several spelling and factual errors and lacked proper attribution for the evidence the author used to reach his conclusions. Key staffers in the campaigns of Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris were also never interviewed.

One person referred to her as "The daughter no one remembers," while another scolded, "You’re a Mom now, don’t act like a teenager."Tiffany's Time to ShineThe Don's youngest daughter married billionaire Michael Boulos at a lavish ceremony and reception at her dad's Mar-a-Lago resort in 2022. The couple originally met in the summer of 2018 at Lindsay Lohan's beach club in Mykonos, Greece.

On May 15, 2025, Tiffany announced the birth of their first child, a son named Alexander Trump Boulos, but the proud grandpa spilled the beans about the pregnancy earlier. 

At a 2024 campaign event in Detroit, President Trump acknowledged several people in the crowd – including Michael's father, Dr. Massad Boulos.

"He happens to be the father of Tiffany's husband, Michael, who's a very exceptional young guy. And she's an exceptional young woman," Trump said before revealing, "And she's going to have a baby. So that's nice."Tiffany Trump's Relationship with Daddy DonaldTiffany, who grew up largely out of the public eye, gained attention when her father began his first presidential campaign.

While there were rumors of a strained relationship with her father, Tiffany maintained they were close, with Donald often encouraging her to focus on her education.

She later gained prominence supporting his presidential campaigns, including his 2024 victory over Vice President Kamala Harris.Tiffany Trump Attended Donald Trump Jr.'s Tropical WeddingTiffany was recently seen in public at brother Donald Trump Jr.'s lavish Bahamas wedding to Bettina Anderson in May. However, her appearance was overshadowed by who wasn't in attendance – particularly their father Donald and younger brother Barron. 

The president's youngest son skipped the tropical celebration entirely while siblings Ivanka Trump, and Eric Trump, joined Tiffany on the islands for the star-studded event.

The president and First Lady Melania Trump were also absent from the ceremony, though insiders claim the newlyweds are hoping to host an additional White House celebration in the future so the couple can attend.

The wedding celebration came after the couple quietly tied the knot days earlier in a private ceremony at the West Palm Beach home of Bettina's sister, Kristina McPherson.

news.title: There are no socialists in power — only personal capitalists
news.text:
Look at the pattern in our own system. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, product of a comfortable intellectual family, secured a prized rent-stabilized apartment while working at a progressive housing nonprofit organization that lives on government grants, a paperwork bureaucracy of case files, compliance forms, and taxpayer-funded advocacy. He was not yet elected, but he was already inside the network that benefits from the controls it expands. Later, as an assemblyman on a six-figure salary, he kept the unit. As mayor, he stacked the rent board and delivered the freeze. The people who profit from these laws often help write them. They design the rules so they can take advantage of the taxpayer without ever breaking the law. The costs do not vanish. They simply appear later as national debt. 

Rent-seeking is the polite term for it. Harry Reid, while Senate majority leader, aggressively promoted a multibillion-dollar solar farm and panel plant in the Nevada desert for a Chinese company, ENN. His son, Rory, a lawyer, represented the firm and helped it lock up thousands of acres of public land at a fraction of appraised value. Family succession fills Senate seats as a matter of course. Lindsey Graham’s sister, Darline, was appointed after his death to finish the term. Jean Carnahan was appointed after her husband’s plane crash and posthumous election. Dynasties transmit networks across generations.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s (D-CA) father and brother were powerful Democratic officeholders before she rose. Early career boosts come through personal relationships with power brokers. Former Vice President Kamala Harris received paid state board appointments from Willie Brown while they were involved. Former first lady Hillary Clinton had never lived in New York. Her Senate seat rested on the national brand of her marriage and the White House years. Politicians’ children receive preferential access to elite schools, jobs, and government-linked contracts. Hunter Biden’s lucrative Ukraine arrangements are only the most publicized example. 

Let’s talk about “Uncle Bernie.” He works on a book advance with guaranteed sales revenue. Campaign committees buy large quantities of the books from the publisher, give them away at rallies and fundraisers, and he still pockets the big checks from advances and royalties. He also routes campaign funds into a family nonprofit organization, the Sanders Institute, founded by his wife and run by his stepson, who draws a six-figure salary. Donor money is converted into personal and family income while the formal rules are carefully observed. The same pattern appears in solar deals, land sales, board appointments, and foundation jobs. The connected design or navigate the system so that the transfer looks legal. When Pelosi says, “We have to do it for the children,” I guarantee her children are going to see more money than it takes for a thousand kids to get K-12 in Alabama. Their children get paid through mechanisms that cost you money. 

Even when rules are broken or bent, the well-connected sometimes appear insulated. Mortgage-fraud allegations against a Federal Reserve governor, a state attorney general, and a sitting senator have produced investigations rather than swift, even-handed accountability. The message is the same: proximity to power changes the consequences. Under the prior administration, the same category of mortgage fraud was prosecuted, and the IRS treated high-end enforcement as a clear priority. Selectivity in who faces the full weight of the law is itself part of the pattern. 

WHEN ‘FREE HEALTHCARE’ CAN’T FIX YOUR JOINT, IT OFFERS YOU EUTHANASIA

Expand the state’s reach over housing, contracts, land, appointments, and lending, and you multiply the opportunities for those who already know how to work the system. We are personal capitalists. But people who use our power to enrich their family, friends, and donors are an organized crime operation, and Social Security makes Bernie Madoff look like a bush-league scrub. The best apartments, the best deals, the best access, the best outcomes for their own. Elect them, and you hand them more leverage. The Pentagon showed me how hierarchy claims the windows with a view. East Berlin showed me how an ideology of equality produces special stores for the connected. Our own politics show the same allocation of the good stuff under democratic clothing. And family dynasties swap from media to government and banks to government and back. The language changes. The reality does not. The bill just gets added to the debt our children will bear. 

Even if socialism worked, it would still be immoral. The hours of your life are yours. If it defends and protects and benefits everyone, then everyone should pay a share. If it benefits individuals on any other characteristic than in trade for their time and service, it is a force-imposed seizure of the hours of a person’s life. If you work anywhere in a non-government-funded job or you work in government as an agent for national security and internal order, you are funding this. It doesn’t work, never has, and that’s the definition of insanity. Repeating something that doesn’t work and makes someone else richer. They take the years, weeks, days, and hours. As in Orwell’s Animal Farm, you get the second serving of your minutes after the pigs get finished at the trough.

Michael Breeden is a retired Air Force chief master sergeant with 29 years of service as a combat controller in special operations. He writes on sovereignty, culture, and institutional accountability.

news.title: Kamala Harris teases adding two new states to US as she addresses 2028 presidential run
news.text:
Kamala Harris has spoken out about running for president again and called for a 'real conversation about revisiting' how certain pivotal US institutions work. 

On July 31, the former Democratic presidential nominee sat down with the National Urban League CEO Marc Morial at the National Urban League Conference in Nashville, Tennessee.

Harris addressed attitude and proposed solutions to certain problems currently facing the United States, whether or not she plans to run for president in the 2028 elections and one particular 'controversial' suggestion when it comes to the Supreme Court and Electoral College.

She said: "We need to revisit the point of expanding the court to 13 justices like we have 13 district courts."

What does the Supreme Court currently look like? 

The Supreme Court of the US is currently made up of nine justices - a chief justice and their nine associates.

While the number of Supreme Court justices is set by Congress, Harris' suggestion would see four more seats added.

Six out of the current nine seats of the Electoral College are currently held by conservative justices - three of whom were appointed by Trump.

Harris continued: "We need to revisit, if they so want, statehood for Puerto Rico and D.C."

What could happen if Washington DC and Puerto Rico become states of the US? 

Washington D.C. is currently a federal district, not a state, while Puerto Rico is an unincorporated US territory.

Given Washington D.C. and Puerto Rico's historical aligning with the left, if they became states of the US this could open up the possibility of a significant electoral advantage for the Democrats.

Allowing a sitting president and Congress to appoint a new majority within the Supreme Court could mean landmark rulings - such as the overturning of Roe v Wade - are easier to control.

Before addressing the layout of the Supreme Court, Harris pre-empted: "I know this is going to be controversial coming from me in particular, we need to revisit the Electoral College."

Indeed, Harris' comment is particularly 'controversial' given the Electoral College has historically been criticized by progressive Democrats with presidential nominees typically swerving discussing it to avoid those who benefit from the system voting against them.

It also follows Harris losing to Trump by 312 votes to 226 in the last presidential elections.

And as to whether she's planning on running for the White House again?

Well, she stated she's 'not made a decision' just yet, adding: "I am fully, sincerely, focused on these midterms."
