news.title: Does the Washington Post Want Democracy to Die in Darkness?
news.text:
The Washington Post sure seems bent out of shape over wealth taxes. And I suppose that makes sense, given that the once-storied publication is owned by one of the five richest dudes on the planet, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, who put the kibosh on the paper’s 2024 endorsement of Kamala Harris, proceeded to kiss the ring of Donald Trump, and has remade the Post’s once-respected opinion section in his own image, declaring in February 2025 that its coverage would henceforth focus on “personal liberties and free markets.” Opinions Editor David Shipley promptly quit, to be replaced by Adam O’Neal, who jumped ship on Friday, citing personal reasons. 

In any case, the Post has been pulling out all the stops when it comes to the wealth tax. They’ve run no less than 10 opinion pieces since March arguing against state and federal taxes on wealth and unrealized income—the “paper” gains that constitute the vast majority of the income of the richest Americans. The fact that the IRS can’t touch that income is how Bezos, according to ProPublica, managed to pay a true income tax rate of less than 1 percent from 2014 to 2018.

Here’s the Post’s recent lineup: • March 2: “Bernie Sanders’s 2028 litmus test would strangle America’s golden goose” (Editorial board)• March 8: “The myth of the billionaire wealth tax” (Megan McCardle)• April 17: “This tax would rain a wealth of unintended consequences” (George Will)• June 5: “The ‘buy, borrow, die’ myth” (Editorial board)• June 27: “Gavin Newsom’s wealth tax two-step” (Editorial board)• July 3: “Lower inequality does not guarantee better democracy” (Editorial board)• July 16: “Socialists think wealth is stolen. They’re wrong.” (Marian L. Tupy, Cato Institute)• July 21: “‘It should be laughed out of the room’: Four writers on midterm ballot measures” (Megan McCardle, again)• July 19: “Medicare-for-all means taxes-for-all” (Editorial board)• July 23: “I’m from Nebraska. Here’s what wealth-tax advocates don’t realize.” (Ben Nelson, former US senator; senior adviser for Saving America’s Family Enterprises)

This last one is particularly problematic for a publication whose editorial slogan is “Democracy Dies in Darkness.” Saving America’s Family Enterprises (SAFE), the organization paying Nelson to promote its talking points, is a “dark money” group—a 501(c)(4) nonprofit that isn’t obligated to disclose who is funding it.

We’ll talk more about SAFE, but first let’s deconstruct this op-ed.

Nelson, an 85-year-old former Nebraska senator, was the Joe Manchin of his time—a Republican in Democrat clothing. Backed by the NRA and the notoriously anti-tax US Chamber of Commerce, he’s a staunch opponent of abortion rights and same sex marriage. More to the point, he was the only Democrat who voted for both of George W. Bush’s tax cut packages—Arlen Specter switched to Democrat only after doing so. In 2009, Nelson was the only Democratic lawmaker to sign Grover Nordquist’s Taxpayer Protection Pledge, a vow to oppose all tax increases.

His big revelation in the Post is that passing any of the proposed federal wealth taxes, or state-level proposals like California’s Billionaire Tax Act ballot measure, would be devastating…for farmers!

Are we stuck in a time warp?

That’s a semi-serious question. As I noted in 2024, and countless others have pointed out before me, the claim that wealth taxes—or the estate tax, in this case—hurts “family farmers” is “a well-worn Republican trope that amounts, fittingly enough, to a heap of cow manure.”

During the 1980s and 1990s, according to an exhaustive analysis published last year in Iowa Law Review, anti-tax zealots “discovered and capitalized upon an incredibly powerful image in the minds of voters: the threat to family farms. Tax opponents authored publications and held hearings detailing ‘family farm horror stories’ involving farms that would potentially have to be sold to pay the estate tax. It turned out not to matter that no policymaker, scholar, or journalist was ever able to uncover an actual example of a family farm that was sold to pay the estate tax.”

“As a factual matter,” notes the paper’s author, Kathleen DeLaney Thomas, a University of North Carolina law school professor and tax expert, “the threat of taxing the family farm out of existence is a myth.”

So, the Post knowingly published a pro-oligarchy opinion piece written on behalf of a dark money group and based on long-ago debunked propaganda, which makes one wonder whether the publishers view the paper’s slogan as aspirational. 

Nelson (or whoever ghost-wrote his op-ed) concedes that most wealth tax proposals only target billionaires, but, he cautions, it’s a slippery slope. He cites a Hoover Institution study that concluded California would ultimately lose $25 billion in tax revenue if this one-time wealth tax passes, because billionaires would flee the state. But is that analysis any good? Not according to a group of prominent economists who support the wealth tax. In their rebuttal, they say the Hoover crew mischaracterized the proposal and made revenue estimates that rely “on a crucial and highly unlikely assumption.”

Speaking of billionaires, how many would actually leave the state? Nobody really knows. Peter Thiel, who purchased citizenship in New Zealand nearly a decade ago and is now reportedly trying to abscond to Argentina, never seemed inclined to remain in California. Allen Prohofsky, a former longtime chief economist for California’s Franchise Tax Board, told me that anyone who claims with certainty that a given tax change will cause an exodus is either lying or “delusional.” 

“The people who really hate, hate, hate taxes? Most of them have already left California,” he says. But for people thinking about it “there’s a host of variables: Where can I get employment? Where does my spouse want to live? What’s the cost of housing?”

“Where are your grandchildren in school? Where is your health provider?” adds Harvey Dale, a tax law professor at New York University who advises billionaire clients in his private practice. Leaving one’s state, or nation, is “a very complicated and ultimately personal decision,” Dale says, “but it doesn’t blend down easily into something simple.”

Nelson’s conclusion: The IRS should simply collect the estimated $700 billion in taxes that go uncollected each year, and that way “farmers wouldn’t be forced to sell their assets.”

Yes! The IRS should do that. But the agency couldn’t manage it even before Donald Trump rose to power. Historically, every time IRS special agents encounter rich Americans who are cheating the government and start digging in, the oligarchs call in favors and next thing you know the agency is defunded again and the investigations are shut down. Trump’s IRS will never collect the money. His minions and (former) trillionaire Elon Musk gutted the agency to such an extent that it can’t even handle basic customer service, as my colleague Stephanie Mencimer recently revealed.

Even the fact we’re talking about Musk in this context should be the most compelling argument for taxing the unrealized gains his wealth was built on. The nation’s growing cadre of billionaires, more now than ever, is exercising vast, undeserved power over public affairs. As Jeffrey Winters, a scholar of oligarchy at Northwestern University, noted in a Mother Jones excerpt of his latest book, Musk was the biggest influencer of federal elections during the 2024 cycle, spending more than $291 million—a fortune for most, but a pittance for him.

What’s more, Winters wrote:

Former Treasury Secretary Andrew Mellon’s grandson Timothy, a man few Americans knew existed, spent about $197 million, and [Sheldon] Adelson’s widow, Miriam, ranked third with more than $148 million. All told, 100 individuals invested $2.4 billion in the 2024 election—almost half the total cost of the presidential contest and 16 percent of all federal election spending. The problem is bipartisan—oligarchs poured money in for Democrats and Republicans alike.

One hundred individuals. Half the presidential election spending. That, my friends, is a democracy killer, which underscores how the Post, with its relentless anti-tax rhetoric, is complicit.

Given that SAFE and its hired gun Ben Nelson want the taxman to collect all of those unpaid taxes, you might think that restoring ample funding for IRS enforcement would be among the group’s goals.

It is not. 

According to IRS filings, SAFE exists “to advocate against federal tax proposals that complicate the tax code, encourage tax avoidance, or harm small businesses, family farmers, homeowners and the middle class.” Indeed, these salt-of-the-earth farmers, concerned young homeowners, and earnest middle-class folks (or actors portraying them) star in some highly misleading videos posted on SAFE’s website to warn against taxing unrealized gains.

One video implies, for example, that someone who buys a $500,000 house could be taxed annually on the increase in the home’s value. That’s completely false. If a couple buys a $500,000 house today and sells it for $1 million after two years—a realized gain, by the way—they won’t owe a dime, because the IRS exempts $250,000 in home-sale profits ($500k for a couple) from taxation.

This aligns with a standard—and false—Republican scare tactic: The IRS is coming for your middle-class family!

So whom does SAFE really represent? It doesn’t disclose its donors, but some clues can be gleaned from its personnel. Its president from June 2023 through May 2026 was Jim Doyle. He’s the owner of Portico Policy Advisors, “a research and strategic communications firm that conducts policy analysis for leading corporations, financial service firms, venture capitalists and nonprofits.” You may recognize some of his clients, like JPMorganChase, Citi, and TPG—an asset management firm with $306 billion under management that offers, among other things, “global wealth solutions.”

And nothing says “middle class” like global wealth solutions.

SAFE’s treasurer is Matthew Mazzanti, a former intern for Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson. Mazzanti, eight years out of college, is also Chief Administration Officer at PPHC, “a family of premier advisory firms specializing in government relations, public affairs, and strategic communications” that includes lobbying shops like Crossroads Strategies, which in 2020 merged with the lobby practice of former Republican House Majority Leader Trent Lott and former Sen. John Breaux (D-La.), both now Crossroads principals and board members. The PPHC conglomerate is led by, in its own words, “established founders and seasoned corporate executives.” It boasts: “Our clients include nearly half of the Fortune 100.”

And I’m sure it’s very concerned with the travails of middle-class America.

In September 2023, SAFE and Breaux co-filed a friend of the court brief in the Supreme Court case Moore v. United States. Like Nelson, Breaux supported the Bush Jr’s 2001 tax cut package. He also sided with a Republican attempt to repeal the estate tax—which the lawyers for America’s upper crust have turned into a punchline. His position on Moore was therefore no surprise; the brief asks the court to rule that taxing unrealized gains is unconstitutional.

It never came to that, because Charles Moore’s gains were in fact realized, the court found, even if the money in question wasn’t distributed to him and his wife. But the opinions of conservative justices in the case shocked many legal observers by making clear that the Roberts court would not tolerate taxes on unrealized gains (Federal wealth taxes are already, for all practical purposes, unconstitutional, as I explained in my recent piece “How to Tax a Billionaire,” though states are not beholden to the federal rules.)

The constitutional issue is really the only decent argument against such a tax—not farmers, logistics, venue-shopping moguls, or the concerns of first-time homeowners with infants. And certainly not to protect the interests anyone below the 90th wealth percentile. The richest 10 percent of Americans, after all, own 87.4 percent of all corporate stock and mutual funds. Most families have little to no unrealized gains—and those would be exempted in any piece of legislation intended to rein in the out-of-control, republic-distorting, oligarchic wealth disparities between affluent households and those just scraping by.

Maybe the Washington Post can just spare us the propaganda next time, and tell the truth: The Roberts Supreme Court, Trump administration, and oligarchs of both parties (including Mr. Bezos), care more about wealth protection than American democracy—would that it survives the present darkness.

news.title: Socialist Kshama Sawant Says AOC's and Progressives' Strategy Isn't Working
news.text: Socialist congressional candidate Kshama Sawant says a recent string of victories by Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates shows voters are hungry for a more confrontational left. In an interview on Saturday ahead of Washington state's top-two primary on Tuesday, Sawant said the lesson from recent socialist wins is not simply that left-wing candidates can win Democratic primaries. It is, she argued, that working-class voters want elected officials willing to break with the Democratic Party itself. "The victories are crucial," Sawant told Newsweek. "They're a positive indication that working people are looking for working-class politics." She said previous elected progressives such as New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have fallen short once in office. "We saw AOC [a New York Democrat] when she first ran. She said that it would be better to be a one-term Congress member than to sell out. That's something I strongly agree with," Sawant said. "Unfortunately, what we have seen people like her do is they have ended up making their own peace with [former House Speaker] Nancy Pelosi and [Senate Minority Leader] Chuck Schumer and other powerful people in the Democratic Party." Sawant, who served on the Seattle City Council for a decade as an independent socialist, is challenging longtime incumbent Democratic Representative Adam Smith in Washington's 9th Congressional District. Washington uses a top-two primary system, meaning all candidates compete on the same ballot regardless of party affiliation, with only the two highest vote-getters advancing to November. The race pits one of Congress' longest-serving Democrats—Smith was elected to Congress in 1996—and the ranking member of the House Armed Services Committee against one of the country's best-known independent socialist politicians, whose campaign centers on opposition to U.S. military aid to Israel, higher wages, universal health care, rent control and taxing wealthy Americans. Sawant argues the political environment has created an opening for an outsider campaign. "Working people are angry at both parties," she said. "They are fed up with being sold out by both parties." Kshama Sawant's Record in Seattle Sawant boasts her track record in Seattle. Driven in large part by her 2013 campaign, when she defeated a Democratic incumbent to win a city council seat, Seattle became the first major city in the United States to implement a $15 minimum wage. If the idea was seen as radical at the time, it did appear to have a domino effect as other major cities and states across the country followed suit. Even Republican-leaning states such as Missouri, and Florida beginning in September 2026, have adopted or are moving to a $15 minimum wage, a position that has become increasingly mainstream within the Democratic Party. Many progressives now float an increase to $25 or even $30 per hour. "Because we won that battle, Seattle's minimum wage is automatically inflation-adjusted and that's why today it is $21.30 an hour, which is the highest in the nation," Sawant said. During her 10 years on the city council, Sawant consistently won reelection despite substantial opposition, including from corporations. In 2019, Amazon, which is headquartered in Seattle, contributed $1.5 million through a political action committee to support her opponent. In 2021, her opponents tried to push her out with a recall campaign, but she survived with just over 50 percent of voters casting ballots in her support. Her grassroots Tax Amazon movement resulted in the 2020 passage of a payroll tax on the top 3 percent of businesses with large payrolls in Seattle. Prior to that she helped push through 2016 legislation capping upfront move-in fees and security deposits for tenants and stronger renter protection legislation. Now she hopes to take the same tactics that helped secure those victories directly to the halls of Congress. Sawant explained that her strategy has been to use her office "to build mass movements, not to make private deals with the Democrats." She believes progressives and democratic socialists have opted for the latter, saying workers "desperately" need fewer "team players" in Congress. "I am not running to be a team player on team genocide or team billionaire or team corporate lobbyist. I am running to disrupt the politics as usual in Washington D.C.," she said. Supporters have credited Sawant with helping push Seattle toward more progressive labor and housing policies as well as building successful grassroots campaigns. Critics, however, have argued that her confrontational style made compromise difficult while some of her proposals risked discouraging business investment and job growth. Sharp Contrast With Adam Smith Sawant drew a stark contrast between herself and Smith, who has represented the district since 1997. Sawant noted that Smith was among the minority of House Democrats who voted in 2002 to authorize military force in Iraq. She also criticized his support for military spending and U.S. assistance to Israel, accusing him of representing corporate interests rather than working-class voters. Smith has rejected such characterizations, describing himself as a progressive Democrat while defending U.S. support for Israel's security alongside humanitarian assistance for Palestinians. Throughout his congressional career, Smith has also argued that his senior position on the Armed Services Committee allows him to shape national security policy while also advancing Democratic priorities on health care, labor rights and other domestic issues. The Democrat has also been sharply critical of Trump's war in Iran. "This war never should have been started, and once it was Trump refused every ceasefire offer on the table. These deaths were preventable and the responsibility sits with him," he wrote on X last week. He also recently voted against a major defense authorization bill. Explaining his decision, he said the bill would give the Pentagon a 60 percent increase, pushing the budget up to $1.6 trillion. He noted on X that this came "at a time when our country is running a nearly $2 trillion deficit. We're doing that while cutting taxes, cutting Medicaid, cutting SNAP, and telling Americans struggling with housing costs that we can't afford to invest in them." Smith hit out directly at Sawant in May after pro-Palestinian protesters planned demonstrations outside his Washington home. He accused his socialist opponent of joining the protests, calling it “unethical and a bastardization of the democratic process.” The incumbent Democrat said that Sawant decided "that intimidating elected officials in their homes is a legitimate way to campaign." Last August, Smith posted with a warning about Sawant's insurgent campaign. "Kshama Sawant, who campaigned against Kamala Harris in 2024, is now targeting me for Congress. She won’t stop Trump’s fascist takeover or fight for our community, but I will," he wrote. Can Kshama Sawant Win? Sawant reiterated in her interview with Newsweek that she's managed to win all of her elections, including the 2021 recall. She attributes that success to the mass movement she was able to create in Seattle. At the same time, she recognizes the election ahead is difficult. Washington has a top-two jungle primary system, meaning all the candidates from every party run against each other in one primary. The two who get the highest number of votes advance and face off head-to-head in the general election in November. "I promise you that if we are in the November election, that will [be] the most electrifying race in the midterm election," she said. "But in order to do that, we need to be one of the top two vote-getters." The district is considered safely Democratic, so a Republican is not expected to win. There is no public polling to provide a snapshot of where each individual candidate stands. But beyond Smith, Sawant is seen to have the best name recognition as well as a history of winning tough Seattle City Council races. According to FEC filings, Sawant has pulled in roughly a third of the amount of money raised by the incumbent Democrat. As of July 15, she had raised just over $645,000 whereas Smith had raked in nearly $1.9 million. Sawant said that she has more than eight times as many individual donors as the incumbent and that her median donation is about $25. She noted that her fundraising is approximately "three times as much money as any of Adam Smith's challengers ever"—pointing out her campaign has managed this even before the general election race. Sawant says while winning is the goal, her "metric of success is not how many elections" she wins. She said elected officials should measure success by victories achieved for workers, even if that creates conflict with established political leadership. "The Democratic and Republican parties both have historically low approval ratings," she said. "Working people are looking for alternatives." The following transcript has been edited for brevity and clarity. Newsweek's Interview With Kshama Sawant For readers who may not be familiar with your political career and what you've accomplished, how did you get into politics, and what did you achieve during your time on the Seattle City Council? I've been a socialist and political activist for about 18 years. In the wake of the Occupy movement, my organization and I agreed that it would make sense to run an election campaign as an independent socialist on really powerful historic demands. It was fundamentally different from how Democratic and Republican politicians become elected officials. They do it for their own careers. We did it democratically through decisions by our membership. news.title: Abdul El-Sayed Chances Against Haley Stevens: Final Michigan Polls
news.text: Michigan's U.S. Senate race is expected to be among the most competitive of the 2026 midterms, and the outcome of the August 4 Democratic primary between Representative Haley Stevens and progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed could prove critical in shaping the contours of the election. Republican Mike Rogers, a former U.S. representative, is the presumptive GOP nominee, but Democrats are set to select either El-Sayed or Stevens to lead them into November in what has become an increasingly contentious primary. El-Sayed is a favorite among progressives, earning endorsements from lawmakers such as New York Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders. Stevens is viewed as the more moderate pick and has the support of Governor Gretchen Whitmer. Regardless of who wins the primary, the race is expected to be competitive in November. Michigan is a critical battleground state that backed President Donald Trump by fewer than 2 percentage points in the 2024 election, so Republicans believe its status as a Trump state gives them a chance at flipping it after Democratic Senator Gary Peters chose not to seek reelection. Democrats are hopeful a favorable national environment driven by Trump’s declining national approval rating will help keep the seat in their hands. Forecasters like the Cook Political Report view the race as a toss-up. Arik Wolk, a spokesperson for Haley’s campaign, told Newsweek that “momentum is at Haley’s back in the final days of the election, as she fights to lower costs, protect Michigan manufacturing, and take on Trump’s corruption and abuses of power.” “Governor Gretchen Whitmer, Senator Gary Peters, former Senator Debbie Stabenow, and so many others are lining up behind Haley because they know she will deliver for Michigan on day one, and she’s the strongest and only Democrat who can beat Mike Rogers. And Rogers knows Haley can beat him too–which is why he said he’d be ‘in great shape’ if Abdul wins the primary,” Wolk said. Newsweek also reached out to El-Sayed's campaigns for comment via email. Abdul El-Sayed vs. Haley Stevens: What Final Polls Show The latest polls of the race gave El-Sayed a lead over Stevens. A survey from Michigan pollster Mitchell Research & Communications, which surveyed 406 likely voters July 28-29, showed El-Sayed up 14 points, 52 percent to 38 percent. His support was boosted by a significant lead with young voters, winning 68 percent of those aged 18-29 and 62 percent of those 30-44. Stevens, however, did best with those 65+, winning 50 percent among that age group. A Zenith Research poll, first reported by Michigan journalist Sam Robinson, found that El-Sayed led Stevens on an initial ballot, 53 percent to 34 percent. When undecided voters were pushed about who they would support, El-Sayed had an 18-point lead, 59 percent to 41 percent. It surveyed 536 likely Democratic primary voters from July 26-30, 2026. An Emerson College poll produced similar results—it showed El-Sayed with a 16-point lead, 57 percent to 41 percent. It surveyed 700 likely voters July 26-27, 2026. A Tavern Research poll showed El-Sayed up 11 points, 48 percent to 37 percent. It surveyed 914 likely voters July 26-27. An earlier poll from Glengariff Group and The Detroit News gave Stevens a 7-point lead, 48 percent to 41 percent. It surveyed 500 likely voters July 8-11. What Do Prediction Markets Show? Prediction markets favor El-Sayed to win the nomination. As of Monday morning, he had a 98 percent chance of winning the nomination on both Kalshi and Polymarket. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always accurately predict the future. Contentious Primary The primary between El-Sayed and Stevens had grown increasingly contentious heading toward primary day. U.S. support for Israel has been a major sticking point in the primary and could continue to be a factor in November, as Michigan is home to notable Arab American and Jewish populations. Many Democrats believe former Vice President Kamala Harris lost votes in the state because of her support for Israel. El-Sayed has cast himself as a critic of the Israeli government, while Stevens has established herself as supportive of Israel and has support from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC). Stevens has also sought to cast herself as the more electable candidate in Michigan, a key swing state, over somebody who is more progressive. The two have traded barbs in recent days. El-Sayed described Stevens as “the least capable candidate in America.” Haley, in response, criticized him in a post to X: “Abdul, we were both on the ballot in 2018. I was capable of winning my competitive primary and general election. You lost. You lost by over twenty points to Gretchen Whitmer and you will lose to Mike Rogers by talking like this. Everyone in America understands you want to blame all of your problems on Jewish Americans,” she wrote. She added that El-Sayed would “just be a celebrity whining and writing books to get even richer” and is “part of the complainer class.” Some Michigan Democrats have declined to say they would support El-Sayed as the nominee. Representative Hillary Scholten, who represents a district based around Grand Rapids, told Semafor that she would “not stand beside someone who has allowed distinctly anti-American sentiment to enter our public dialogue.” That leaves Tuesday's winner with a pivotal task of uniting the party divided by such a contentious primary. Michigan Is Democrats' Must-Win State Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, so Democrats must flip four seats to win control. A Republican victory in Michigan would complicate Democrats’ path. Democrats are defending a seat in another Trump-won state, Georgia, where Senator Jon Ossoff is running for reelection. Democrats also view GOP-held states in Maine, which Trump lost by 7 points in 2024, and North Carolina, which he won by 3 points, as top flip opportunities. But there are no other Senate races in Harris-won or single-digit Trump states, meaning Democrats have to expand the Senate battleground and compete in more conservative areas if they want to win the majority. They are targeting GOP-held seats in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas as potential states to flip. The Cook Political Report classifies races in Alaska, Maine, Michigan and Ohio as tossups. Prediction markets favor Republicans to keep control of the Senate. The GOP had a 53 percent chance on both Kalshi and a 56 percent chance on Polymarket of holding on to its majority as of Monday. Michigan Could Become Next Progressive Test An El-Sayed victory would set up Michigan to become a major test for the political left in the midterms. Progressive representation in the House and Senate is primarily confined to safe Democratic seats, but a surge in progressive support in primaries this cycle gives them an opportunity to expand their reach into more competitive territory. The Wisconsin governor's race, where state legislator Francesca Hong has carved out a polling lead, could be another key test for the left, as it’s another state that narrowly backed Trump in 2024. So far in the primaries, progressive candidates Brad Lander, Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier won House primaries in New York. In Colorado, progressive Melat Kiros unseated Representative Diana DeGette in the Democratic primary for a Denver-based House seat, while state legislator Julie Gonzales came close to defeating Senator John Hickenlooper in the primary. How Michigan Became Swing State Michigan has become an electoral battleground over the past decade. Former President Barack Obama easily won the state twice—by more than 16 points in 2008 and by just under 10 points in 2012. But Trump flipped it in 2016, carrying it by less than half a percentage point. Trump made gains across the state because of his strong showing among white voters in rural areas who backed Obama. He lost ground in the suburbs around Detroit and Grand Rapids, but rural gains made up for it. Democrats struggled to win back those voters in significant numbers in recent cycles but continued to make gains in the suburbs. Michigan flipped back to Democrats in 2020, when former President Joe Biden carried it by just under 2 points. But Trump won it again in 2024 by about 1.4 points—the strongest showing for a Republican presidential candidate since 1988. At the same time, Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin won an open seat by less than half a percentage point in 2024. Michigan was particularly tricky for Democrats in 2024. Harris lost significant ground among Michigan’s large Arab American community, many of whom declined to support her because of the Biden administration’s strong support for Israel amid the conflict in Gaza. Winning back those voters will be critical for whichever Democrat emerges from the Senate primary, as Democrats cannot afford to lose Michigan in November. news.title: AP Decision Notes: What to expect in Missouri’s state primary
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A St. Louis-area congressman faces a Democratic primary rematch Tuesday against the former congresswoman he previously ousted, a showdown that has again drawn the attention of a powerful pro-Israel organization.

The contest, as well as primaries for Missouri’s seven other U.S. House seats, will be the first held since Republican state lawmakers adopted a new congressional map backed by President Donald Trump that was designed to boost their party’s chances of keeping control of the chamber in November’s midterm elections.

In the St. Louis-based 1st Congressional District, freshman Democratic U.S. Rep. Wesley Bell seeks a second term. He must first clear a strong primary challenge from his predecessor, former U.S. Rep. Cori Bush, who was a member of the group of progressive House members known as The Squad.

Bell defeated Bush in the 2024 primary by nearly 6 percentage points with the help of about $8.6 million in outside spending from the political arm of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, which promotes U.S.-Israel relations. Bush has been a vocal critic of Israel since its response to the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack. The committee spent about $3.1 million in July against Bush and in support of Bell ahead of Tuesday’s primary.

The district is heavily Democratic. Democratic then-Vice President Kamala Harris received about 78% of the district vote in her unsuccessful 2024 presidential run against Trump.

On the other side of the state, Democratic U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver is running for a 12th term on much different turf than the compact, Kansas City-based district he’s represented for more than 20 years. The Republican-controlled state Legislature’s mid-decade redistricting plan carved up heavily Democratic Kansas City among three districts and stretched what remained of Cleaver’s 5th Congressional District eastward to pick up heavily Republican areas. Cleaver is now running in a district that Trump carried with about 58% of the vote, compared with the current 5th District, which supported Harris with about 61% of the vote.

The six Republicans running to challenge Cleaver in November include former Boone County Clerk Taylor Burks, state Sen. Rick Brattin and former law professor Brett Hueffmeier. Burks led the Republican field in fundraising, more than tripling Brattin in both money raised and cash in the bank as of mid-July.

Voters will also decide the fates of four statewide ballot measures, including one that would make it harder to pass citizen-driven proposals to amend the state constitution and another that would eliminate the state income tax.

Amendment 4 would change the vote threshold required to pass voter-initiated ballot measures to amend the state constitution. Currently, only a simple statewide majority is needed to approve a constitutional amendment put on the ballot by voters. If Amendment 4 passes, a voter-initiated proposal would require a vote majority in each of the state’s congressional districts.

Amendment 5 would require the state Legislature to phase out individual income taxes in Missouri and expand sales taxes.

About half of Missouri’s 34 state Senate seats and all 163 state House seats are up for election in 2026. Republicans hold roughly 2-1 ratio majorities in both chambers.

Here are some of the key facts about the election and data points the AP Decision Team will monitor as the votes are tallied:

When do polls close?

Polls close at 7 p.m. CT, which is 8 p.m. ET.

What’s on the ballot?

The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare winners in contested primaries for U.S. House, state auditor, state Senate and state House, as well as in four statewide ballot measures.

Who gets to vote?

Any eligible voter may participate in any party’s primary.

How many voters are there?

As of the 2024 general election, there were 4.4 million registered voters in Missouri.

How many people actually vote?

About 586,000 Republican primary votes and about 322,000 Democratic primary votes were cast in the 2022 primaries for state auditor.

By comparison, about 698,000 Republican votes and about 379,000 Democratic votes were cast in the 2024 primaries for governor.

How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot?

About 12% of the vote in the 2024 state primary was cast early in person or by mail. Missouri does not have a long tradition of pre-Election Day voting. The state began allowing no-excuse early voting in the 2022 general election.

When are early and absentee votes released?

Local election officials tend to release all or almost all results from mail and early in-person voting in the first vote update of the night. In roughly half of Missouri’s counties, they are released along with some results from in-person Election Day voting. But the state’s most populous jurisdictions tend to release very few in-person Election Day results in the first vote update.

How long does vote-counting usually take?

In the 2024 state primaries, the AP first reported results at 8:06 p.m. ET, or six minutes after polls closed. The vote count surpassed the halfway mark at about 10:20 p.m. ET. The last vote update of the night was at 12:26 a.m. ET, with about 99.9% of total votes counted.

When will the AP declare a winner?

The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why.

How do recounts work?

Missouri does not have automatic recounts, but candidates for federal, judicial and state offices, including state Legislature, may request a recount if the margin is less than 0.5% of the vote. Candidates for local offices may request a recount if the margin is less than 1% of the vote. A court may also order a recount as part of an election contest proceeding. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.

Are we there yet?

As of Tuesday, there will be 91 days until the 2026 midterm elections.

Follow the AP’s coverage of the 2026 election at https://apnews.com/projects/elections-2026/.

How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot? 

About 12% of the vote in the 2024 state primary was cast early in person or by mail. Missouri does not have a long tradition of pre-Election Day voting. The state began allowing no-excuse early voting in the 2022 general election.

When are early and absentee votes released?

Local election officials tend to release all or almost all results from mail and early in-person voting in the first vote update of the night. In roughly half of Missouri’s counties, they are released along with some results from in-person Election Day voting. But the state’s most populous jurisdictions tend to release very few in-person Election Day results in the first vote update.

How long does vote-counting usually take?

In the 2024 state primaries, the AP first reported results at 8:06 p.m. ET, or six minutes after polls closed. The vote count surpassed the halfway mark at about 10:20 p.m. ET. The last vote update of the night was at 12:26 a.m. ET, with about 99.9% of total votes counted.

When will the AP declare a winner?

The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why.

How do recounts work?

Missouri does not have automatic recounts, but candidates for federal, judicial and state offices, including state Legislature, may request a recount if the margin is less than 0.5% of the vote. Candidates for local offices may request a recount if the margin is less than 1% of the vote. A court may also order a recount as part of an election contest proceeding. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.

Are we there yet?

As of Tuesday, there will be 91 days until the 2026 midterm elections.

news.title: AP Decision Notes: What to expect in Washington state's primary
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Nine contenders for one of the nation’s most hotly contested congressional seats will compete in the Washington state primary on Tuesday for two spots on the November general election ballot. Voters across Washington will also choose finalists for the state’s nine other congressional seats, as well as for the state Legislature and state Supreme Court.

Democratic U.S. Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez is running for reelection for the 3rd Congressional District seat she first won narrowly in 2022. A former auto shop co-owner, she is the best-known and best-funded of the four Democrats on the ballot. She also faces challenges from three Republicans, including state Senate Minority Leader John Braun, who has a key endorsement from President Donald Trump. The southwest Washington district is expected to be a key U.S. House battleground this fall.

Washington state has a top-two primary system in which all candidates compete on the same ballot and the two highest vote-getters regardless of party advance to the general election.

The 3rd Congressional District borders Oregon to the south and the Pacific Ocean to the west. Trump received 50.3% of the vote from 3rd District voters in 2024, besting the 47% Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris received. Gluesenkamp Perez received 50.1% of the vote in the 2022 general election and about 52% in 2024.

Incumbents are running for reelection in nine of the state’s 10 congressional districts. The exception is the 4th Congressional District, where Republican U.S. Rep. Dan Newhouse is retiring after six terms. Newhouse was among 10 House Republicans who voted to impeach Trump following the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol by a mob of his supporters.

Eleven candidates are running to replace him, including Yakima County Commissioner Amanda McKinney and entrepreneur and former NASCAR driver Jerrod Sessler, both Republicans. Trump endorsed McKinney in January on the five-year anniversary of the insurrection. He previously endorsed Sessler’s unsuccessful bid to unseat Newhouse in 2024. Trump received 59% of the 4th District vote in the presidential election that year.

About half of Washington’s 49 state Senate seats and all 98 state House seats are up in 2026. Democrats currently control about 60% of seats in each chamber.

Three of Washington’s nine state Supreme Court justices are on Tuesday’s ballot, including Chief Justice Debra Stephens. A fourth seat is open. Although state Supreme Court seats are nonpartisan, liberals hold a majority and the ideological balance of the court is not at stake.

Here are some of the key facts about the election and data points the AP Decision Team will monitor as the votes are tallied:

When do polls close?

In-person voting centers close at 8 p.m. PT, which is 11 p.m. ET.

What’s on the ballot?

The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare winners in contested primaries for U.S. House, state Senate, state House and state Supreme Court.

Who gets to vote?

Any eligible voter may participate in the state’s top-two primary system.

How many voters are there?

As of July 1, there were about 5.1 million registered voters in Washington.

How many people actually vote?

About 2 million votes were cast in the 2024 all-party primary for governor. That was slightly higher than the roughly 1.9 million votes cast in the 2022 all-party U.S. Senate primary.

How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot?

Washington conducts its elections almost entirely by mail, and very few voters cast their votes in person. In the 2024 state primary, about 58.5% of voters delivered their ballots to a drop box, while about 41.3% sent their ballots through the mail.

As of Thursday, about 699,000 ballots had already been cast in Tuesday’s election.

When are early and absentee votes released?

The first vote updates of the night tend to include mostly results from mail voting with relatively few results from early in-person or in-person Election Day voting. A handful of counties, including two of the more populous in the state, Spokane and Clark, often release the bulk of their absentee results in their first vote update, but most counties roll them out over the course of the night.

How long does vote-counting usually take?

In the 2024 state primary, the AP first reported results at 11:06 p.m. ET, or six minutes after polls closed. The last vote update of the night was at 11:43 p.m. ET, with about 51% of total votes counted. The vote count surpassed the 75% mark on the Thursday following the election at 7:56 p.m. ET and reached about 95% of the total vote six days after the election at 7:24 p.m. ET.

When will the AP declare a winner?

The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why.

How do recounts work?

Machine recounts in Washington state are automatic if the vote margin between the top two candidates is less than 2,000 votes and less than 0.5% of the total votes cast for both candidates. Manual recounts are required for statewide contests if the margin is less than 1,000 votes and less than 0.25% of the total votes cast for both candidates. For all other races, manual recounts are required when the margin is less than 150 votes and less than 0.25% of the total votes cast for both candidates. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.

Are we there yet?

As of Tuesday, there will be 91 days until the 2026 midterm elections.

Follow the AP’s coverage of the 2026 election at https://apnews.com/projects/elections-2026/.

news.title: Kamala Harris wants to expand the Supreme Court and rethink the Electoral College
news.text:
Kamala Harris is openly weighing another White House run and says she hasn't ruled out a 2028 presidential campaign. 

Harris is calling for a major shake-up of the U.S. political system, including expanding the Supreme Court from nine to 13 justices.

She also wants Puerto Rico and Washington, D.C., admitted as states and says it's time to rethink the Electoral College after her 2024 defeat.

While keeping 2028 on the table, Harris says her immediate priority is helping Democrats win key races in this year's midterm elections.

news.title: Kamala Harris teases adding two states to US and expanding Supreme Court as she mulls another White House run
news.text:
Former Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris has called for two more states to be added to the union and for the expansion of the Supreme Court as she mulls another run for the White House.

Harris, 61, the ex-California attorney general and senator, was former president Joe Biden’s deputy during his single term in the Oval Office before running in his stead against Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election, narrowly losing.

She has remained involved with Democratic politics since that disappointment and told the National Urban League conference in Nashville, Tennessee, she had plenty of ideas for resolving the problems of the United States.

“We must allow for a real conversation about revisiting certain things,” Harris told her audience. 

“For example, I know this is going to be controversial coming from me in particular, we need to revisit the Electoral College,” she said, alluding to the fact that she lost it to Trump by 312 votes to 226 – as well as the popular vote by 49.8 percent to 48.3 percent.

“We need to revisit the point of expanding the court to 13 justices like we have 13 district courts,” Harris continued. “We need to revisit, if they so want, statehood for Puerto Rico and D.C.”

The Supreme Court has only nine justices, a chief justice and their nine associates, and, currently, a clear right-leaning political bias as three of its judges were nominated by Trump, which an expansion would help to dilute.

Puerto Rico, meanwhile, is presently designated a U.S. territory and D.C. is a federal district, meaning that neither is entitled to a state’s rights, despite the pivotal role both locations play in American life and culture.

Trump has likewise talked about expanding the union during his second term, regularly imploring Canada to become the 51st state, a gesture that has been angrily rebuffed by the U.S.’s neighbor to the north.

Elsewhere in her address to the NUL, Harris said had “not made a decision” on a potential 2028 presidential run.

“I am fully, sincerely, focused on these midterms,” she told the audience, nodding to her campaigning efforts on behalf of such candidates as James Talarico, who is running for the Senate in Texas against the Lone Star State’s scandal-blighted attorney general Ken Paxton.

The former vice president also stressed the importance of “having an agenda that is about turning out the vote in the greatest numbers we have ever seen so that… in this environment where they are cheating, we will be too big to rig.

“It means being ruthless. They are ruthless. We need to be ruthless, too. And by that, I do not mean cruel. That is not our nature. 

“By that, I do not mean breaking the law. That is not what we do. But I do mean we must be uncompromising.”

Harris – who last year wrote a memoir about the short time she had to prepare to face Trump, entitled 107 Days – was speaking in a moment in which voters now routinely express buyer’s remorse over the Republican’s return to power. 

Voters often tell pollsters they disapprove of his wayward war with Iran and handling of the economy as his approval ratings sag.

The president is widely felt to have failed to deliver on his promise to create a new “golden age” of wealth and prosperity for Americans, which could come back to bite his party in November’s midterms, potentially handing control of the House of Representatives and even the Senate to Democrats.

If that were to happen, Trump would face the prospect of spending his final two years in the Oval Office as a lame duck, his legislative agenda frustrated on Capitol Hill and the threat of investigation hanging over what remains of his presidency.
news.summary: Former Democratic presidential nominee calls for major reforms to America’s institutions but says she has ‘not made a decision’ on whether to launch another bid for the Oval Office

news.title: What Midterms Polling Reveals 3 Months Before Election Day
news.text: President Donald Trump’s historic, norm-breaking presidency has unraveled Washington and thrown the Democratic Party into a state of shock. However, after what’ll be two years of relative powerlessness, in three months' time, Democrats have a chance to take back control of Congress and counter Trump's agenda. The RealClear Polling Generic Congressional vote gives Democrats a 6-point edge. Kalshi and Polymarket give the party an 86-84 percent chance of taking the House, but Republicans still hold a 56-54 percent chance of keeping the Senate. Of course, in today’s era of politics, anything can happen, and both parties have reasons to feel confident. "While Democrats are busy infighting and nominating candidates with severe character flaws, Republicans are united, on offense, and armed with the largest war chest in party history,” Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary for the Republican National Committee (RNC), told Newsweek in a statement. "President Trump has lowered drug prices, secured our border, created jobs, and lowered taxes—and he’s just getting started. It’s a clear choice between common sense versus communism in November, and we're confident our voters will turn out to give President Trump a full four years to implement his America First agenda.” However, Democrats believe that not only do national polls and prediction markets point in their direction, but lower-profile elections since Trump returned to office demonstrate measurable voter resistance to Replican policies. Speaking to Newsweek, a DNC official pointed to Democratic performance in special elections and state legislative races as evidence that voter enthusiasm and early organizing may matter as much as headline cash-on-hand figures. "Donald Trump and Republicans have created a toxic midterm environment for themselves by driving up costs on everything from gas to groceries to healthcare, leaving Americans feeling like they’re barely able to keep their heads above water," DNC spokesperson Jaelin O’Halloran told Newsweek in a statement. "While Trump and Republicans leave Americans grappling with their reckless tariffs and a deadly and costly war with Iran, Democrat candidates are on the ground, showing up and listening to voters about the issues that matter most. Since Trump took office, Democrats have been aggressively organizing and investing across the country to help our candidates win up and down the ballot—and that’s why Democrats are going to sweep this November.” However, as Newsweek has been charting daily in our Midterms Monitor newsletter, there is more to these races than just the overall national narrative, and each contest has idiosyncrasies and polling quirks that shape whether they lean left or right. Newsweek crafted a breakdown of the nine Senate races and 18 House races that will determine control of Congress. Senate Conventional wisdom suggests Republicans hold an advantage when it comes to controlling the upper chamber after this cycle, as Democrats path to victory runs through state's that Trump won firmly each of the three times he's run. To attain the gavel, the left must net four seats. With just three months, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) and National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) each hold strategies they believe will deliver control. For Republicans, the strategy hinges in part on winning Michigan. "As Democrats drown in dysfunction and burn resources on divisive primaries in Michigan and Minnesota, Senate Republicans remain focused on exposing the socialist, tax-hiking agenda of candidates like Abdul El-Sayed,” NRSC national press secretary Bernadette Breslin told Newsweek. Meanwhile, DSCC Chair Joe Bush shared the following statement from DSCC Chair Kirsten Gillibrand on why she believes Democrats hold an edge: "While Democrats run on local issues, lowering costs, and fighting for working families, Republicans’ batch of weakened, flawed candidates are being put on defense for their records and support of Trump’s toxic agenda that is spiking prices, ripping away health care, and putting billionaires and powerful special interests before the American people.” Here are the individual dynamics shaping each race that dictate which candidates currently hold a polling lead: Alaska Trump has won Alaska three times, and the state is not considered a swing at the presidential level. Nonetheless, in former Congresswoman Mary Peltola, Democrats see one of their best fighters in their quest to take control of the Senate. Incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan has $8 million in cash while Peltola has $6 million, but the race remains complicated. An independent candidate, who also happens to be named Dan Sullivan, will appear on the state’s ranked-choice ballot. Also, Peltola has won statewide before, with her "Fish, Family, Freedom” motto being widely known in the state, but she’ll need to work hard to knock off the Republican candidate. Cook rates the race as a toss-up, and in turn polling is mixed, with some showing Peltola a few points ahead and others giving Sullivan a slight lead. Prediction market Kalshi gives Peltola a 55 percent chance of flipping the seat while Polymarket gives her a 61 percent chance. If the markets prove correct, a Peltola victory would send shock waves through the political system and shift the narrative about Democratic competitiveness in red states. Maine Perhaps no race in the country has offered as many twists and turns as Maine. Political outsider Graham Platner created shock waves by beating Governor Janet Mills in the Democratic primary by drawing on his unorthodox background as Newsweek reported in May. However, following allegations of rape and sexual misconduct, he dropped out of the race, and former State Senate Leader Troy Jackson rose in his stead, promoting a similarly populist message. "Democrats are fighting for the [working class],” Jackson told Newsweek. "We just need to get back to [talking] economics.” In theory, he should be poised for victory. Maine has voted against Trump each time he ran, after all. Yet, he faces five-term Senator Susan Collins, who notably knocked off a Democratic challenger in 2020 despite Trump losing the state. She chairs the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee and controls an $11 million war chest to boot. Cook rates this contest as a toss-up, and polling on the race is limited and mixed. However, Kalshi gives Jackson a 64 percent chance of winning, and Polymarket gives him a 68 percent chance. As in 2020, where Collins trailed in nearly every poll, Maine is a hard state to gauge, which means Democrats and Republicans will be taking this race very seriously in the build-up toward November. Michigan Michigan remains undecided on the Democratic side, with former state public health official Dr. Abdul El-Sayed facing Congresswoman Haley Stevens in an August 4 primary in what’s become a key proxy between the Democratic establishment and the progressive wing of the party. Meanwhile, former Congressman Mike Rogers has been sitting tight as the GOP’s presumptive nominee for months. Rogers came within 0.3 percent of beating Congresswoman Elissa Slotkin in 2024 for that cycle’s open Senate seat. The seat being fought over now is held by retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters. Though Michigan has not elected a Republican to the Senate since Spencer Abraham won an open seat in 1994, this race has emerged as a "very good pickup opportunity” for the party, given the contentious Democratic primary and relatively short window between the primary and Election Day, a GOP official told Newsweek. In turn, Cook rates this contest as lean D. In the RealClear Polling averages, El-Sayed polls 0.5 percent ahead of Rogers, and Stevens also polls 0.5 percent ahead. Polymarket gives Democrats a 68 percent advantage while Kalshi gives Democrats a 69 percent chance. While Democrats have an edge, the closeness of these races in an expected blue wave year reflects their unique dynamics. "We’re running a campaign to Get Michigan Working Again, which means reviving Michigan manufacturing, saving our schools, securing our streets, and making life more affordable,” Rogers told Newsweek. Ohio This is the only race this cycle that effectively pits two incumbents against each other. The senator in office, Jon Husted, has served since 2025 after being appointed to Vice President JD Vance’s former seat. But he’s up against former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, who served in the Senate for 18 years but lost his seat in 2025 to Bernie Moreno. With Trump no longer atop the ballot, Brown believes he can win despite the state’s red hue. His campaign manager Patrick Eisenhauer previewed this message in Newsweek's Midterms Monitor: "Ohioans across the state are fed up with skyrocketing costs and Jon Husted voting to make things worse,” Eisenhauer, said adding that families were ready to hold Husted “accountable for his role in the affordability crisis." Husted spokesperson Amy Natoce countered with this message: "Sherrod Brown spent 32 years in Washington with nothing to show for it. Polls will go up and down all summer. What won’t change is that voters fired Brown two years ago after looking at this record, and they’re not willing to go backwards now.” Cook rates it a toss-up, and RealClear Polling gives Brown a 0.6 percent advantage. Polymarket favors Brown by 52 percent, and Kalshi favors him by 53 percent. Democratic turnout and 2024 regret among swing voters will determine the race. Georgia The race to represent Georgia in the U.S. Senate pits incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff against incumbent Republican Congressman Mike Collins. While many considered this match to be the race where Democrats were most vulnerable entering the cycle, most election forecasters agree that’s no longer the case. The Cook Political Report shifted this race from toss-up to "lean D” in May, but the RealClear Polling average places Ossoff nearly eight points ahead. Kalshi gives Ossoff a 90 percent chance while Polymarket gives him 88 percent. Part of that comes on account of Ossoff’s $42 million war chest, while Collins has just around $2 million in cash on hand. The other part lies in the fact that Ossoff has generated significant excitement among Democrats, so much so that he’s being touted as a potential 2028 presidential candidate. "I think that people are getting excited about him because he does not back down from Donald Trump," Maria Cardona, a Democratic strategist and CNN commentator, told Newsweek in a July profile of Ossoff’s momentum. North Carolina The race to flip North Carolina was supposed to be a far tougher task for Democrats. This was the only swing state Trump carried in each of his three presidential runs, and the state has not elected a Democratic senator since 2008. Nonetheless, former Governor Roy Cooper is running away with it, posting a near 8-point RealClear Polling lead and a "lean D” rating from the Cook Political Report. Kalshi gives Cooper a 91 percent chance while Polymarket gives him 88 percent. This seat is currently occupied by Republican Senator Thom Tillis, who Trump threatened with a primary. Tillis elected to retire, and in his stead emerged former RNC Chair Michael Whatley. Despite that role, Whatley has struggled with fundraising. The former chair has just $3.5 million in the bank compared with Cooper’s $20 million. As far as pickup opportunities go, North Carolina stands as the Democrats' best opportunity. "A lot of North Carolina voters, including Republicans and independents, feel like they know Roy Cooper's character and appreciate his pushback against the tax breaks for billionaires and health care cuts that Whatley supports,” Andrew Bates, a Democratic strategist and native North Carolinian, told Newsweek. "At the same time, Whatley will have a flood of corporate money behind him, and it's been almost 20 years since a Democrat won a Senate race there, which is why we know this race will be incredibly close." New Hampshire With the retirement of longtime Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen, New Hampshire boasts an open seat. Trump lost the state in each of his presidential runs, but both parties still consider it a swing state, and that’s reflected in the numbers. The RealClear Polling average places Democratic Congressman Chris Pappas 3 points above former Republican Senator John E. Sununu. The prediction markets are a bit more bullish for Democrats, with Kalshi giving Pappas an 87 percent chance and Polymarket offering 84 percent. Politicos on both sides of the aisle acknowledge that in an ideal world, Republicans would have recruited John’s brother, Chris Sununu, the state’s popular former governor. Nonetheless, the Sununu name has a long history in the state, with their father John H. Sununu having served as the state’s governor and their mother Nancy Sununu having served as chair of the state Republican Party. Though this race may not be the splashiest, it’s a defensive opportunity Democrats are taking seriously. As outlined recently in Newsweek’s Midterms Monitor, New Hampshire is part of the DSCC’s $40 million "Win the Senate" program. "New Hampshire’s purple. It was Kamala Harris’ closest state, and the Sununu name has been a household name for a long time since before I was born,” Pappas told PunchBowl News. "It’s going to be incredibly tricky.” Iowa Barack Obama won Iowa in 2012, but since then the state has become firmly red, with just one Democrat (State Auditor and 2026 gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand) holding statewide office. However, with Trump holding a sub-40 approval rating, Democrats believe this could be their year to make inroads. The race to replace retiring Senator Joni Ernst pits Republican Congresswoman Ashley Hinson against State Representative Josh Turek. In most years, Hinson’s candidacy in Iowa would go unquestioned. She’s raised $6.75 million compared with Turek's $2.36 million and has had an uncontroversial tenure in the House while holding a seat on the powerful Appropriations Committee. However, with Trump facing low approval and Turek boasting a unique resume as a Paralympic gold medalist with the U.S. men's national wheelchair basketball team, Democrats are hopeful for an upset. Cook still rates the race as "Lean R” and RealClear Polling has the race as a tie. Prediction markets are a bit more confident in Hinson, however. Kalshi gives her a 57 percent chance of winning, and Polymarket gives her a 56 percent shot. Texas Perhaps no race has captured the imagination of Democrats more than Texas. State Representative James Talarico, a seminarian, has captured the party with his charismatic speeches and confident TV appearances, raising nearly $69 million in the process. Meanwhile, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, is a MAGA darling who’s overcome a litany of scandals and opposition from the party establishment, which Newsweek has covered closely. Paxton has raised just over $9 million this cycle, per Texas Tribune. Texas is the crown jewel among GOP-controlled states and has not been represented by a Democrat in the Senate since 1993. Cook rates the race as Lean R, and the NRSC does not have it among its list of battlegrounds, which includes the eight other listed races. Despite that, the RealClear Polling average has Talarico leading by 0.9 percent. Kalshi has Paxton at a 53 percent chance of winning, and Polymarket gives him a 52 percent chance. No victory would be a greater shock to the political ecosystem this year than for Talarico to win in Texas. If he proved Democrats can win their statewide races, the GOP would face serious questions about its ability to maintain a winning coalition. House Prediction Markets Show A Democratic Edge The House battlefield is harder to read than the Senate map because many competitive districts have little recent public polling, with the races featuring a greater emphasis on local and regional issues. Prediction markets offer a live, if imperfect, signal of where traders think these races stand, and at the time of writing, the available market data showed Democrats ahead in every House race reviewed by Newsweek. That matters because the chamber is closely divided. “Democrats are running on lowering costs for the American people and ending the culture of corruption and self-dealing that leaves working people behind,” Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) Spokesperson Liam Buckley told Newsweek. “House Republicans don’t work for everyday families, they work for billionaires and special interests — it’s why they broke their promise to bring down prices and instead slashed health care and cut taxes for the wealthy and well-connected. The American people are with us, that’s why Democrats will win the House in November.” Naturally, the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC) rejects this narrative, believing that not only will the GOP House’s record carry candidates to victory but the natural political climate of the races in play favors their party as well. "House Republicans are running on a winning agenda of tax relief for working families, lower costs, secure borders, safer communities, while Democrats are increasingly consumed by a civil war over the radical socialist takeover of their party,” NRCC Spokesman Mike Marinella told Newsweek. “The NRCC has the stronger candidates, the more favorable map, record-breaking fundraising, and a winning message, while the DCCC is bogged down by self-inflicted chaos after wasting millions on disastrous far-left primaries and turning on one another." Cook Political Report lists 18 House races as Toss Ups, including several of the districts below. Here are what pollsters and the oddsmakers say about each of the 18 crucial races: Arizona: Two GOP-held Seats Where Markets Lean Democratic In Arizona's 1st congressional district, at the time of writing, Kalshi priced Democrat Amish Shah at 75 percent and Republican Jay Feely at 25 percent. Polymarket showed a similar picture, with Shah at 73 percent and Feely at 28 percent. Sponsored by Kalshi In Arizona's 6th congressional district, Kalshi priced Democrat JoAnna Mendoza at 83 percent and Republican Juan Ciscomani at 17 percent. Sponsored by Kalshi Both Arizona districts are rated Toss Ups by Cook Political Report and Inside Elections, so the contrast is useful: forecasters still see highly competitive races, while the markets clearly tilt toward Democrats. California: CA-22 Shows A Forecaster-Market Split In California's 22nd congressional district, Kalshi priced Democrat Randy Villegas at 80 percent and Republican David Valadao at 20 percent. Polymarket had the Democratic Party at 83 percent and the Republican Party at 15 percent. Sponsored by Kalshi This is one of the clearest examples of markets being more bullish on Democrats than some forecasters. Cook Political Report rates CA-22 as a Toss Up, while Inside Elections places it in Tilt Republican. Colorado: CO-08 Looks Like A Core Battleground In Colorado's 8th congressional district, Kalshi priced Democrat Manny Rutinel at 74 percent and Republican Gabe Evans at 26 percent. Polymarket had Democrats at 71 percent and Republicans at 23 percent. Sponsored by Kalshi Both Cook Political Report and Inside Elections rate CO-08 as a Toss Up, making it a clean example of a race that forecasters still treat as genuinely competitive even as markets lean Democratic. A Republican source told Newsweek that districts like this are unlikely to produce "a massive victory margin either way,” even when one party appears favored in market data. The source pointed to Evans’ local profile, including agriculture and ranching, as a reason Republicans believe he remains well-matched to the district. Evans’ official House site says his family operates a farm in southern Weld County and describes CO-08 as a hub for agriculture, food processing, transportation and energy production. Florida: FL-25 Is A More Cautious Democratic Signal Florida's 25th congressional district is one of the closer market reads. Kalshi had Democrats at 63 percent and Republicans at 35 percent, while Polymarket had Democrats at 61 percent and Republicans at 37 percent. Sponsored by Kalshi Inside Elections rates FL-25 as a Toss-up, so this should be viewed as a Democratic edge in the markets, but not a commanding one. New Jersey: NJ-07 Points To Suburban Pressure On Republicans In New Jersey's 7th congressional district, Kalshi priced Democrat Rebecca Bennett at 84 percent and Republican Thomas Kean Jr. at 21 percent. Polymarket had Democrats at 79 percent and Republicans at 19 percent. Sponsored by Kalshi In some races, the market prices do not add up cleanly to 100 percent, so they are best read as a directional signal: traders were pricing Democrats ahead, not producing a traditional polling-style probability. Cook Political Report rates NJ-07 as a Toss Up, while Inside Elections lists it as Tilt Democratic. New York: NY-17 Shows The Same Tension In New York's 17th congressional district, Kalshi priced Democrat Cait Conley at 68 percent and Republican Mike Lawler at 32 percent. Polymarket had Democrats at 79 percent and Republicans at 19 percent. Sponsored by Kalshi The market numbers suggest traders see a Democratic opportunity, but the forecasters remain more cautious. Cook Political Report and Inside Elections both rate NY-17 as a Toss Up. Pennsylvania: Three Toss Ups, Different Market Margins Pennsylvania may be the most important House cluster in this list, with its 7th, 8th and 10th congressional districts all rated Toss Ups by Cook Political Report and Inside Elections. In PA-07, Kalshi priced Democrat Bob Brooks at 71 percent and Republican Ryan Mackenzie at 33 percent. Polymarket had Democrats at 77 percent and Republicans at 24 percent. Sponsored by Kalshi PA-08 looked tighter. Kalshi priced Democrat Paige Cognetti at 62 percent and Republican Rob Bresnahan at 43 percent, while Polymarket had Democrats at 57 percent and Republicans at 43 percent. Sponsored by Kalshi PA-10 showed a stronger Democratic market position. Kalshi priced Democrat Janelle Stelson at 76 percent and Republican Scott Perry at 18 percent, while Polymarket had Democrats at 79 percent and Republicans at 22 percent. Sponsored by Kalshi The overall Pennsylvania takeaway is that all three races are competitive on the ratings board, but not identical in the markets: PA-08 appears closer, while PA-10 looked more favorable to Democrats at the time of writing. Virginia: One Of The Strongest Democratic Market Readings In Virginia's 2nd congressional district, Kalshi had Democrats at 81 percent and Republicans at 18 percent. Polymarket had Democrats at 84 percent and Republicans at 16 percent. Sponsored by Kalshi That is one of the strongest Democratic readings in the market data, even though Cook Political Report and Inside Elections both rate VA-02 as a Toss Up. Washington: WA-03 Remains Competitive In Washington’s 3rd District, Kalshi showed the Democratic Party ahead of the Republican Party in its House winner market, with Democrats at 84 percent and Republicans at 23 percent at the time of writing. Sponsored by Kalshi Forecasters remain cautious. Inside Elections rates WA-03 as a Toss-up, underscoring that Democratic incumbent Marie Gluesenkamp Perez is still facing a competitive race despite the market’s Democratic lean. Wisconsin: WI-03 Is Democratic-leaning But Still Competitive In Wisconsin's 3rd congressional district, Kalshi had Democrats at 63 percent and Republicans at 35 percent. Polymarket had Democrats at 67 percent and Republicans at 34 percent. Sponsored by Kalshi Both Cook Political Report and Inside Elections rate WI-03 as a Toss Up. That makes it more like FL-25 and PA-08 than VA-02: the markets lean Democratic, but not so strongly that the race should be treated as settled. What Happens Next? Taken together, prediction markets show a House battlefield that looks more favorable to Democrats than the Toss Up ratings alone suggest. The clearest Democratic market advantages appear in AZ-06, NJ-07, VA-02, WA-03, CA-22 and PA-10, while FL-25, PA-08 and WI-03 look closer. But the markets do not make these races settled. They show Democrats being priced ahead in districts forecasters still consider competitive. If those markets are wrong, the reason may lie in the same caution reflected by nonpartisan race ratings: district-level polling is limited, local dynamics matter, and late campaign developments can still move voters. Despite being statewide, these dynamics shape Senate races as well. With three months till November 3, expect an avalanche of campaign dollars as each party seeks to win over the small but pivotal population of swing voters who will decide the election and shape the course of America’s future.
