news.title: Inside the Michigan Senate primary that could reshape the Democratic Party
news.text:
FERNDALE, Mich. — “Money out of–” Abdul El-Sayed called out to the hundred or so people who turned out to a get-out-the-vote event in the closing days of the Michigan Democratic Senate primary.

“Politics!” they shouted back.

“Money in your–”

In a few words, that call-and-response summed up El-Sayed’s whole campaign: as much a run against Rep. Haley Stevens as against the political system as a whole. “This is ‘the money’ versus ‘the many,’” he told MS NOW backstage just before the event. 

Tuesday's primary is the latest test of whether progressive policy and messaging can survive Democratic voters' anxieties about electability — and it's playing out in a seat the party almost certainly must win to have any shot at retaking the Senate. This intraparty brawl will say as much about who’s best positioned to “fight” for Michigan as it does about the future of the Democratic Party.

El-Sayed casts himself as a political outsider, bucking the “progressive” label and actively correcting the “democratic socialist” sometimes applied to him — he’s not a socialist, even as he’s boosted by, and sounds like, many of the people who wear that banner: Sen. Bernie Sanders, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Hasan Piker, the leftist streamer and commentator.

This kind of firebrand, anti-establishment populism has found pockets of support in Michigan before, but not enough to win statewide.

Electability concerns dog him, too. Republicans say they'd rather face El-Sayed in November — even as some late polls show him pulling ahead of Stevens. He told MS NOW that he'll beat the GOP standard-bearer, Mike Rogers, "by seven [points], probably more” in November. 

Other Democrats are less optimistic. Though a Republican hasn’t won a Senate election here in more than three decades, in 2024, Rogers came within about 0.3 percentage points of defeating now-Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a Democrat widely known as a political moderate.

It’s a cautionary data point Stevens has been quick to press. Rogers, she says, “believes Abdul will make it easier for him to win,” while pushing her own credentials as “a tough-as-nails Democrat … who wins for Michigan.” Like Slotkin, she was first elected to the House in 2018 while flipping a swing seat from red to blue. She has held it since, even as its boundaries were redrawn to make it safely blue.

“I could have stayed comfortable,” she told a predominantly Black congregation on a recent Sunday while campaigning. “I could have stayed in that House seat that we all worked so hard for. You know, the first pro-labor, pro-voting rights Democrat in 50 years to get that seat. I could have stayed comfortable, but this is not the moment to stay comfortable, is it?”

Stevens is counting on Black voters across Michigan to fuel her — especially in Detroit, the Democratic stronghold and state’s most populous city. But she’s also got the backing of Michiganders who themselves have won tough statewide races in the perpetual battleground state, including Sen. Gary Peters, who holds the seat, former Sen. Debbie Stabenow and sitting Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. Peters and Whitmer previously said they were not going to endorse, only to be drawn off the sidelines as El-Sayed’s momentum grew.

“The change of heart is that we know we have to hold Michigan,” Peters told MS NOW after endorsing Stevens last month.

The Gaza question

Many Democratic primaries turn on differences of style and message. This one has that dynamic, but features major disagreements on policy — chief among them, U.S. support for Israel. Michigan has large Muslim and Arab populations sympathetic to the Palestinian cause, while pro-Israel Jewish voters have long been important backers of the Democratic Party. For many voters on both sides of that issue, it is deeply personal — which helps explain why, in 2024, a small but potentially decisive number of voters here stayed home or withheld their support for Vice President Kamala Harris over her stance on Gaza. Trump carried the state.

El-Sayed has been sharp critic of Israel, accusing the U.S. ally of committing genocide in Gaza and saying he’d vote to halt more American dollars going to aid it.

“I don't pay my taxes — you don't pay your taxes — so other countries get bombs and tanks for no reason,” he told MS NOW. 

Asked how that instinct — spend at home, not abroad — would apply to something like aid to Ukraine, El-Sayed drew a distinction: “What I'm against is unconditional foreign military aid. Ukraine aid is not unconditional. We’re not just funding the military of Ukraine because we want to; we're funding the Ukrainian military because they are actively fighting a war against a guy who transgressed against their boundaries. That’s conditions.”

Stevens takes a more traditional approach, calling for a two-state solution and a permanent ceasefire. While she has criticized Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, last month, she voted against a House bill to halt $3.3 billion in funding for Israel — a measure more than 100 House Democrats supported, in a vote that laid bare how far the party has moved amid years of outrage over Gaza, much of that outrage concentrated in Michigan. 

Asked whether anything might make her rethink her posture on Israel, Stevens demurred.

“I'm running for a six-year term, and that is certainly a long runway for issues to continue to evolve,” Stevens told MS NOW. “I saw my vote the other day as moving us closer to the goal of peace. I want the U.S. and Israel to be working together to get aid into Gaza, to get rebuilding resources into Lebanon.”

Looming over the fight — and the race, writ large — is outside money. More than $75 million in advertising spending has poured into the primary, according to AdImpact, and 80 percent of it has supported Stevens, including about $30 million from a super PAC tied to the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC.

El-Sayed has made that number the centerpiece of his case against her.

“They don't spend $60 million to elect somebody unless there’s a pro quo at the end of that quid,” El-Sayed told MS NOW. “I want to get money out of politics — because our politics should be about us.”

Stevens denies the money would influence her votes in the Senate. She has pointed to a super PAC supporting El-Sayed’s campaign largely funded by his father-in-law, Jukaku Tayeb.

“I don't think there's much difference between super PACs going in for Abdul or super PACs going in for me,” Stevens said during a July debate. 

On the broader issue that's the centerpiece of her opponent’s campaign, though? “We have a problem with campaign finance reform in this country,” she said.

That is an existential question for Democrats, who have tried to run on campaign finance before and lost, but who wonder whether this moment of disenchantment — with Washington, and with the way things have always been done — is finally an inflection point.

“You have to ask the fundamental question: What does it mean to be a Democrat?” said Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., here campaigning for El-Sayed. “And the answer to that, in my view, needs to be about working people. It needs to be about creating opportunity. It needs to be about fairness.”

Asked what it means if the voters’ answer Tuesday isn’t El-Sayed, Warren — who has vowed to back the ultimate nominee here — said plainly: “Money talks.”

Lillie Boudreaux contributed to this article

news.title: Did Trump Rig the 2024 Election? What the Viral Videos Claim, and What the Evidence Actually Shows
news.text: Viral clips claiming President Donald Trump confessed to rigging the 2024 US election have drawn millions of views, but fact-checkers who traced each video back to its source reached the same verdict. He never admitted it.What the Videos Actually ShowThe clips spread fastest in early 2025 and have resurfaced online repeatedly since. One, viewed millions of times on X within days, showed Trump seated in the Oval Office saying 'they rigged the election, and I became president'. Captions insisted the president had confessed on camera, and the post jumped across Instagram, Threads, TikTok, and Facebook.The footage was real. The framing was not. The clip came from a 7 March 2025 signing event with Fédération Internationale de Football Association (FIFA) President Gianni Infantino, where Trump discussed the 2026 World Cup coming to North America. PolitiFact, part of the Poynter Institute, parsed the full exchange and rated the confession claim False.He was recycling his long-debunked grievance about 2020, not describing how he won 2024.The distortion works because the raw quote sounds damning on its own. Strip away the World Cup context and the year he is referencing, add an urgent 'PLEASE SHARE' caption, and a rambling aside becomes a headline. That is the mechanic behind nearly every version of this claim.A Pattern of Miscontextualised ClipsThis was not the first time his words were clipped and relabelled. Almost identical claims followed a 19 January 2025 pre-inauguration rally, when Trump told supporters he would be in office for the 2026 World Cup and the 2028 Olympics. Fact-checkers again found no admission, only his familiar and false framing of the last contest he actually lost.Each viral 'confession' traces back to Trump talking about 2020, an election he lost to Joe Biden and still insists was stolen without proof, rather than the 2024 race he won outright.Where Real Questions End and Speculation BeginsDocumented concerns about 2024 do exist, though they sit far from anything Trump has said. Election-integrity groups including the Election Truth Alliance and SMART Elections have flagged statistical patterns, among them unusual vote drop-off in Nevada. In parts of Rockland County, New York, they note some districts logged almost no presidential votes for Kamala Harris even where residents backed other Democrats elsewhere on the ballot. Both groups have filed lawsuits and pushed for hand recounts.Independent reporting describes those findings as speculative and so far unproven. Official reviews have pointed the other way. Michigan's Bureau of Elections said a statewide audit found a 33-vote difference between machine and hand counts across millions of ballots, a result it presented as confirming the accuracy of the original tally.Why the Distortion Matters to YouWatchdogs warn the real damage is cumulative. Repeated rigging claims, whether aimed at 2020 or 2024, and whether amplified by Trump or by his critics, chip away at public confidence even when no tampering is found. As of July 2026, the weight of reporting and expert fact-checking still finds no credible evidence that anyone rigged the 2024 vote in Trump's favour.For anyone scrolling past the next clip, the test is quick. Check which election Trump is actually talking about, and check who verified the video, before hitting share.
news.author: Jim Manzon
